h: Margaret Hamilton, who led the code that landed Apollo 11 and named "software engineering", dies at 90
t: She was the Apollo project's first programmer at MIT and went on to lead more than 400 people. Her idea of software that expects mistakes is now how everyone builds it. Hamilton, born in Paoli, Indiana, in 1936, studied mathematics and came to Boston in 1959 while her husband studied law. A temporary job writing weather-prediction software for the MIT meteorologist Edward Lorenz was her way into programming; her work fed into his later papers on chaos theory. At Lincoln Laboratory she wrote code for SAGE, America's first air-defence system, and began to think about software reliability, then a barely explored idea. In 1965 her husband spotted a newspaper advert: MIT's Instrumentation Lab wanted people to write software to "send man to the moon". She was hired as the project's first programmer, and its first woman programmer. By 1968 she was assistant director in charge of the Command and Service Module team. When her four-year-old daughter Lauren crashed the simulator by starting the pre-launch program P01 in mid-flight, Hamilton asked for a safeguard and was told astronauts would never do that. On Apollo 8, Jim Lovell did, and her fix went in. In July 1969, moments before Eagle touched down, the guidance computer raised a 1202 alarm: it was overloaded. Her team's priority-driven software dropped background jobs to keep the landing tasks running, and Houston trusted it enough to let Armstrong and Aldrin land. She began calling it "software engineering" to win the work the same respect as hardware; at first, she said, "it was considered to be quite amusing". She founded Higher Order Software in 1976 and later Hamilton Technologies, wrote more than 130 papers, and received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016. The Apollo code went up on GitHub in 2015; Lego made her a minifigure in 2017. A memorial will be held in Cambridge in the spring.
s: MIT News · BBC · Cambridge, Massachusetts · died 30 September, announced 7 October

h: The high-speed line may now take the land it needs between Porto and Oiã
t: The Diário da República has published the order letting AVAN Norte, the concession company building the Porto–Oiã section of the Lisbon–Porto high-speed line, take administrative possession of the plots on its route. The secretary of state's order declares the land of public utility, the step that allows works to start before compensation is settled. The section runs south from Porto through the Ovar concelho to Oiã, near Oliveira do Bairro. Landowners with questions can visit the line's mobile help centre, which was in Arada on Wednesday and answers questions on the route and on which properties are affected.

h: Fifty-one travel films from 25 countries come to Ovar
t: The 19th ART&TUR tourism film festival runs from 27 to 30 October at the Escola de Artes e Ofícios, chosen from 247 entries. Entry is free with registration; the last day tours tiles, pão-de-ló and the cooperage.

h: A national VAT-fraud raid reaches the Aveiro district
t: "Operação Hermes" by the Polícia Judiciária's northern directorate led to 39 arrests over a scheme trading phones and electronics; more than €300 million in assets were frozen.

h: The electric São Jacinto ferry is up for an EU-funds prize
t: The Salicórnia, which carries 260 passengers and 19 cars across to Forte da Barra, is a finalist in the "Portugal + Conectado" category.

h: A new M20 tram will loop round the old Tegel terminal
t: The BVG's tender sketches seven kilometres and eleven stops from Jungfernheide to Kurt-Schumacher-Platz, every five minutes at peak, serving 20,000 jobs and 5,000 flats planned at Tegel. Approval is due only by April 2032.

h: Four Brandenburg colleges may now award doctorates themselves
t: Eberswalde, FH Potsdam, TH Brandenburg and TH Wildau share the right through a joint doctoral college; 40 candidates start this winter semester.

h: German output jumped 2.0% in August, four times the forecast
t: Construction led with +9.3%, despite low water on the Rhine. It is the strongest rise since March 2025, after July's 1.2% fall.

h: A steel tendon has snapped inside the Rudolf-Wissell bridge, Berlin's busiest stretch of autobahn
t: The Autobahn GmbH closed the two outer lanes of the 930-metre bridge that carries the A100 city motorway over the Spree on Wednesday, after first checks found a broken external tendon in one of its hollow box girders. The tendons squeeze the prestressed concrete together so it does not crack under traffic; with one gone, the bridge probably no longer carries its full design load, said the company's Jan-Felix Mühe, though there is no immediate danger because many other tendons hold it. The tendon will be rebuilt over the next weeks, and a static survey is set to last until 21 October. The bridge takes up to 180,000 vehicles a day, on what rbb calls Germany's third-busiest motorway section, but the company expects no extra chaos: only two lanes reach the closed stretch anyway. Spalled concrete reported earlier came from elsewhere on the bridge and is unrelated.

h: The 2027 budget goes to parliament this afternoon, two days early
t: The cabinet approves the proposal this morning; finance minister Joaquim Miranda Sarmento hands it in at 14:15 and presents it at 16:00. The legal deadline would have been Monday, since 10 October falls on a Saturday. Sarmento has promised a surplus of 0.1% to 0.2% of GDP and growth of about 2%, and says income-tax relief in 2027 will come through updated brackets. Passage is already assured by the Socialists' abstention. MPs debate it in principle on 27 and 28 October; the final vote is set for 24 November.

h: Test trains run on the Linha Rosa
t: Metro do Porto has begun running vehicles on the new São Bento–Casa da Música line, almost half a year before it is due to open; the company has named March 2027.

h: A working group wants the law changed to protect Porto's historic centre
t: The architects the city appointed in July, after ICOMOS raised alarm over works in the UNESCO zone, propose a "heritage alert" to catch problems early.

h: The North added 37,200 jobs in a year
t: Unemployment fell to 5.7%, the lowest since 2022, says the CCDR-N. Construction led with 16,500 more workers; farming lost 9,500. Average pay reached €1,289.

h: Wildlife is down 73%, but the lynx is back, says the WWF
t: The Living Planet Report keeps its average decline, but for the first time lists recoveries; WWF Portugal cites the Iberian lynx and the sardine. Tigers rose from 3,200 to 5,700 since 2010.

h: Chrome 155 will display JPEG XL, with a decoder written in Rust
t: Google is shipping decoding for the .jxl format from Chrome 155, years after pulling an earlier experiment. The Chrome team says JPEG XL compresses 30–50% better than JPEG and adds lossless compression, built-in HDR and lossless re-encoding of existing JPEGs. Because image decoders parse untrusted bytes straight from the network, a classic target for memory bugs, the new one is written in Rust. Google's advice to web developers: try both AVIF and JPEG XL. It expects JPEG XL to win for high-fidelity or lossless photos and where fine-grained progressive loading matters.

h: GPT-6 arrives, and ChatGPT starts answering with interfaces
t: "Intelligent UI" lets answers include charts, diagrams, forms and buttons, or small tools such as a bill splitter, built inline. It is rolling out to all users.

h: Sorkin returns to Facebook in The Social Reckoning (2026), and critics split
m: Drama · 1h 52m · cinemas from 9 Oct · RT 64%
t: Sixteen years after The Social Network, Aaron Sorkin directs his own follow-up. Mikey Madison plays whistleblower Frances Haugen and Jeremy Allen White the Wall Street Journal's Jeff Horowitz, whose Facebook Files showed the company knew it was fuelling division; Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg. Sony opens it worldwide on 9 October, and Público has already reviewed it under its Portuguese title, O Veredicto Social. The Film Stage calls it an effective thriller that "can't stick the landing"; IndieWire calls it agitprop with a lousy script. Too new for an IMDb rating.

m: Documentary · c. 6h · RT 100%
t: Julia Loktev follows her Russian dissident journalists into exile after the Oscar-shortlisted first part. IndieWire: "gripping".

h: Rich collectors have started asking AI what to buy
t: The Art Basel & UBS survey, out today, polled 3,100 wealthy collectors in ten markets. In 2024 just 4% used apps or AI tools for advice; now 22% do, about evenly across generations. Gen Z spends most, an average of $347,460 on art in 2025 against $124,265 for all ages, and is also the most private: 39% show their collections only to family and close friends. Painting is still the usual first purchase (43%), and only 1% bought a work over $1 million. Family is the commonest way in, 40% for Gen Z.

h: Portugal's culture workers will strike on 17 October
t: The performers' and musicians' union CENA-STE wants better pay and to free its members for the CGTP's national march in Lisbon, Porto and Coimbra.

h: A Soviet guitar found in Porto becomes an album about exile, with Alexander Hacke
m: Music & spoken word · Tradisom · Stella · out this month
t: Journalist and illustrator Pedro Sousa Pereira learned that a Stella electric guitar, made in the Soviet Union and sold, smuggled and rebuilt along the way, had ended up in Porto. Its story became Stella, by the Porto collective Grémio: music, field recordings and spoken word about dictatorships, war and refugees. The players include Guilherme Lucas, João Nieto (The Crystal Cabinet) and Luís Vaz Patto, with the Englishman Rick Blackman and, from Berlin, Danielle de Picciotto and former Einstürzende Neubauten bassist Alexander Hacke.

h: Eighteen months in prison for bot-streaming AI songs
t: Michael Smith, 54, used up to 10,000 fake accounts from 2017 and must forfeit $8 million in royalties: the first US prison term for streaming fraud.

t: Founder Jesper Kouthoofd told Highsnobiety he announced the plan in a reorganisation last autumn. The OP-1 made the Swedish firm's name in 2011.

h: Avatar: Seven Havens (2026) brings a new Avatar after Korra
m: Animated fantasy series · Book 1: 13 half-hour episodes · Paramount+ · from 9 Oct
t: Michael Dante DiMartino and Bryan Konietzko, who made The Last Airbender and The Legend of Korra, return for Nickelodeon's Avatar Studios. In a world broken by a cataclysm, Pavi, a young Earthbender, learns she is the Avatar after Korra; hunted by humans and spirits, she and her long-lost twin Nisha must uncover where they came from and save the Seven Havens. Saheli Khan voices Pavi and Aishu Devan Nisha. Paramount+ drops three episodes on Friday and three more each week until the last four on 30 October; a second book of 13 is confirmed but undated. These are the announced premiere dates; check your local Paramount+. No ratings yet.

t: She was 87, carried out on a stretcher on 23 September from the Madrid flat she had lived in for 70 years. Campers in Puerta del Sol held a minute's silence and marched to Congress.

h: Houthi missiles and drones kill three at two Saudi airports
t: Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority says two women, from Morocco and Algeria, were killed and 28 people wounded at Abha airport near the Yemeni border, and a Sudanese man was killed and eight wounded at King Khalid International in Riyadh, in attacks on 6 and 7 October. The Houthis' spokesman Yahya Saree claimed both with ballistic missiles and drones, calling them a reply to "60 airstrikes and missile attacks in the past 24 hours", and said they also hit Aden's airport. It is an escalation of Yemen's renewed civil war, in which the Iran-backed Houthis recently seized stretches of the Red Sea coast, including the port of Mokha.

h: The AfD wins a German parliament's chair for the first time, with four votes nobody owns up to
t: Tobias Rausch was elected president of Saxony-Anhalt's state parliament with 48 of 82 votes. The AfD and its new BSW allies have 44 seats. In Berlin, the SPD wants the CDU to explain the rest. At the first sitting of the parliament elected on 6 September, the AfD's Tobias Rausch, 35, won in the first round: 48 votes for, 29 against, five abstentions, with 82 of the 83 members present. The AfD, which won the election with 43.8% but no majority, holds 39 seats. The five MPs of the BSW, which renamed itself on 1 October, had promised their votes. That still leaves at least four votes from the CDU, SPD, Greens or Left. The SPD, Greens and Left, 22 MPs together, had said they would vote no; the CDU leadership told its 15 MPs to abstain, but only five abstentions were cast. Because the rules don't count abstentions, the CDU's plan lowered the bar anyway: a majority of yes-and-no votes was enough. The state's intelligence service has classed the Saxony-Anhalt AfD as confirmed right-wing extremist since 2023. As president, Rausch runs the sittings, hands out reprimands, holds police powers in the parliament's buildings and hires and moves its staff. He was himself reprimanded in 2024, and he was criticised earlier this year over nepotism. Later the same day his party colleague Hans-Thomas Tillschneider became vice-president, and the SPD candidate failed. In Berlin, SPD MPs marched from the Bundestag through the Brandenburg Gate to Bebelplatz, where the Nazis burned books in 1933, and Boris Pistorius started the national anthem. Klingbeil and general secretary Tim Klüssendorf want the CDU, their coalition partner, to say who voted for Rausch. CDU parliamentary leader Thorsten Frei said in a secret ballot "anyone" could have. The pressure falls on Sven Schulze, the CDU's acting premier, whose group did not follow him. AfD leader Ulrich Siegmund will stand for premier in December and says he will find the votes. Brandenburg, where the AfD could also come first, is already debating whether its parliament's rules need changing.

h: Aveiro's farm fair goes ahead without its cattle, for fear of a disease in Spain
t: Agrovouga 2026 runs from 14 to 18 October, but with no cattle on show. There will be no live Friesian dairy cow and no national contest for the Marinhoa, the local breed raised mostly on farms in the Baixo Vouga and Mondego. The breeders' associations chose to stay away after cases of lumpy skin disease in Spain. No outbreak is known in Portugal, but Elizabete Pires of the Aveiro dairy-cattle support association says gathering animals from many farms is not advisable now. The Marinhoa will still feature through a producers' conference and food tastings, and horses take the main stage. The fair has also moved: it used to be held in November and is now half as long. Last year bird flu disrupted it. Entry is free.
s: Notícias de Aveiro · Câmara Municipal de Aveiro

t: Most cuts hit Aveiro–Águeda–Sernada. Track is being renewed with millions in public money, but breakdowns and staff shortages keep trains off the narrow-gauge line.

t: An idealista ranking on PriceLabs data puts the median night at €191, with a pool at 41% of places. Mafra tops the list.

t: Sanctions stopped Russia's Monarch Group paying, and the site has been idle for almost four years. t: That puts Berlin 14th of the 40 biggest cities, level with Munich, at the end of 2025. Mannheim leads with 60.6%. The BVG says it was near 20% by May, and a third by 2027.

h: A former head of the BND is arrested on suspicion of treason
t: Federal police arrested August Hanning, 80, BND president from 1998 to 2005, at his home near Münster on Tuesday, and his former office chief Manfred D. in Bavaria; homes and offices in Berlin were also searched. Prosecutors say D., who ran the office of successive BND presidents until March 2026, passed Hanning about 2,000 documents for money. Many were briefings for the weekly security meeting at the Chancellery, reportedly on Iran's nuclear programme, the Russian army and material from partner services. Hanning is suspected of using them to write at least one analysis for a foreign intelligence service; WDR, NDR and the Süddeutsche report it was not Russia. Investigators found the papers while searching his house in 2025 over the attempted abduction of businesswoman Christina Block's children, which he denies taking part in. A judge at the Federal Court of Justice decides on custody today. No former German official this senior has ever been accused of treason.

h: The Socialists will let Montenegro's 2027 budget pass
t: The PS confirmed on Tuesday that it will abstain on the 2027 state budget, enough to get it through whatever the rest of the opposition does. The party's André Moz Caldas said the country must not start the year on duodécimos, the month-by-month spending used when no budget is passed; the PS says it wants to avoid a "political precipice". Party leader José Luís Carneiro had proposed abstention after assurances from the prime minister, including on the constitutional revision. Finance minister Joaquim Miranda Sarmento forecasts a surplus of just 0.1% to 0.2% of GDP and warns that unfunded opposition measures could push the accounts into deficit. The PS says it may change its vote if the government springs surprises.

h: Attackers hijacked three country domains to get fake TLS certificates for Google
t: Google said on Tuesday that attackers took over the .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone) and .as (American Samoa) top-level domains and changed the authoritative DNS records for selected names inside them. Controlling DNS let them pass the automated domain checks that certificate authorities use, and obtain certificates for "several Google domains" and other big brands and services. With such a certificate an attacker can impersonate the real site even over HTTPS. Google has updated Chrome to block every unauthorised certificate it found and worked with the issuing authorities to revoke those for its own properties. The case shows the weak link in the chain: a certificate is only as safe as the DNS behind it.

h: Mistral Large 4, "le Chonk", is the Paris lab's biggest model yet
t: One trillion parameters, 49 billion active, trained on 3,800 Grace Blackwell GPUs. It beats open rivals but trails OpenAI and Anthropic on coding. Open weights due late October.

h: Paramount closes its Warner takeover, and HBO Max will merge with Paramount+
t: The $111 billion deal was completed on Tuesday. The combined company is called Skydance, after David Ellison's studio. It ends a saga that began when Netflix announced its own bid for Warner Bros. Discovery last year, then dropped it in February. Skydance says HBO Max, Paramount+ and Discovery+ "will unify into a single service over time", with no date or price yet. Ellison wants his film chiefs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein to deliver 30 films a year; an eighth Transformers, with Steven Spielberg as executive producer, may be the first. The deal has raised fears of job cuts in Hollywood and, the BBC asks, higher prices.

h: Thieves take Dalí's 150-kilo bronze cover of the "world's heaviest book"
t: The cover of the Livre de l'Apocalypse, bronze set with precious stones, seashells and, this being Dalí, cutlery, was stolen on Sunday night from a small private museum in Issoire, central France. The book was made between 1958 and 1961 by the publisher Joseph Forêt with contributions from Cocteau, Buffet, Foujita, Fini, Zadkine and Giono; Picasso refused to join if Dalí did. Its 150 sheepskin pages were not on display and are safe. Complete, it weighs about 210 kilos and was once valued at two million francs. The thieves broke the gate and the display case. "They assassinated France last night," said its owner, the restorer Christian Karoutzos.

h: France's school strike spreads to parents, students and unions
t: The government counted more than 250,000 marchers on Tuesday and disruption at 891 lycées, almost a quarter of the total; student unions said 450,000 and 1,800 schools blockaded on what they call "Act Three". Teenagers marched from Place de la République in Paris demanding money for crumbling schools and less police force. Police used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, though there was less trouble than before. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says 215 students, 85 staff and 715 police officers have been hurt since the protests began. After an emergency cabinet meeting the education ministry ordered schools to reopen gradually from today.

k: Berlin · Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine
h: A Berlin algae researcher shares the Nobel Prize for switching brain cells on with light
t: Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University, Georg Nagel of Würzburg and Karl Deisseroth of Stanford share the 2026 prize for optogenetics. It began with a single-celled alga and how it finds the light. The Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet gave this year's prize in physiology or medicine to Karl Deisseroth (born 1971) of Stanford University and the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, Peter Hegemann (born 1954) of Humboldt University of Berlin, and Georg Nagel (born 1953) of the University of Würzburg, "for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics". The 12 million Swedish kronor are shared equally. Hegemann and Nagel did the prize-winning work at Max Planck institutes in Martinsried and Frankfurt. It started with Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, a single-celled green alga that swims towards light. When its gene sequences became public around 2000, Hegemann's group found genes resembling known light-sensing proteins. Nagel put the proteins into frog eggs, and together they showed that one, channelrhodopsin-2, is an ion channel opened directly by light. When blue light hits it, charged particles flow into the cell and create an electrical signal, whatever cell it sits in. Deisseroth put the gene into rat nerve cells and fired them with short pulses of light, published in 2005. Two years later the switch worked in the brains of living mice. Researchers can now turn chosen neurons on or off and watch what changes, testing whether a group of cells actually causes a movement, a feeling or a memory. Francis Crick had suggested light for exactly this in the late 1970s. The first medical use is in the eye. Hegemann says a first patient who regained a simple kind of sight was presented in 2021. In September the US FDA accepted for review a gene therapy for retinitis pigmentosa with severe sight loss; it is not yet approved. Hegemann learned of the prize from an email from the committee chair asking him to call. "Of course I was overwhelmed," he told rbb24. He has also said: "You have to take risks."
s: Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet · tagesschau · rbb24 · Ars Technica · 5 October

h: The Barrinha opens to the sea and leaves hundreds of fish on Esmoriz beach
t: Hundreds of small fish lay on the sand at Praia de Esmoriz, next to the Barrinha, on Monday after the lagoon's channel to the sea was opened. Locals say they are pumpkinseed sunfish (perca-sol, Lepomis gibbosus), an invasive species from North America that thrives in calm fresh water. The Barrinha de Esmoriz, or Lagoa de Paramos, lies between Ovar and Espinho and connects to the ocean only from time to time. When the bar opens, the lagoon empties into the sea in a strong surge, and OvarNews says that current probably carried the fish out to the river mouth and onto the beach. Walkers also found many sea hares, known locally as "vinagreiras", on the sand. The lagoon is a Natura 2000 site because of the range of species it holds.

h: Aveiro's port has its plan for a bigger harbour entrance
t: The design would cut back one breakwater and extend another so larger ships can enter. Port president Teresa Cardoso says an environmental impact study comes next. The 2013 works opened the bar to ships up to 200 m long and 10.5 m draught.

h: An Ovar walker writes up his Camino de Santiago
t: Miguel Costa presented his first book, "Quando Menos É Mais", at the municipal library on Friday. It tells of his walk along the French Way to Santiago and is published by Primeiro Capítulo.

h: The Tiergarten tunnel will close four nights a week for lack of staff
t: Only five of the eight posts in the control room are filled, and three of those staff are ill or in training. Until further notice the tunnel shuts from about 21:45 to 05:45 on the nights into Tuesday through Friday. Buses M41 and M85 are diverted. Berlin has had to staff the control room itself since federal oversight ended at the end of 2024.

h: The BND chief says Russia is waging a "shadow war" on Germany
t: At their yearly public hearing, Martin Jäger listed intimidation, cyberattacks and prepared sabotage. A year ago he spoke of an "icy peace"; now he warns Germany itself could be drawn into a violent confrontation.

h: The navy gets a second North Sea port, in Emden
t: Boris Pistorius signed for berths for seven frigates, ten minehunters and ten tugs and up to 2,000 posts, ready in the early 2030s. "The smallest navy in the Bundeswehr's history," he said, "must grow."

h: Shida Bazyar wins the German Book Prize for "Die Lücken"
t: The Berlin-based writer, born in 1988, tells nearly 100 years of a small Hunsrück town, from the 1920s on, through a dead narrator. She said she found it hard to feel joy over a book about people who were persecuted and murdered.

h: Requests to refuse military service have tripled since the new Wehrdienst law
t: Between January and August, 12,102 people applied to be recognised as conscientious objectors, the federal office for civil-society tasks (BAFzA) told the RND newspapers. That is already three times as many as in the whole of 2025, when there were 3,879, and more than five times the 2,249 of 2024. At the end of June the count stood at 5,862, so it has doubled in two months. Conscription is still suspended, but the new military service law took effect on 1 January and makes medical screening compulsory for young men born in 2008 or later. If too few volunteers come forward, the Bundestag can vote for "conscription on demand". Applications come from reservists and serving soldiers as well as from people who have never served, and counselling centres report rising demand. The right to refuse is in Article 4 of the Basic Law and applies whether or not conscription is active; it needs a written, personal justification.

h: Mitsubishi Fuso moves its European headquarters to Portugal
t: The Japanese truck maker will run imports, sales, after-sales and marketing for 41 European markets from Portugal, along with a European parts distribution centre and development of its Canter and electric eCanter trucks. The new centre replaces the one Daimler Truck ran and will employ 40 people, about 30 of them in new jobs. Its base is the Tramagal plant near Abrantes, for 46 years Fuso's only factory in Europe. It opened in 1964 building French Berliet trucks under licence and has made Mitsubishi vehicles since 1980. In April Fuso merged with Toyota's Hino into Archion, in which Daimler Truck and Toyota hold 25% each. The plant restarted production in September with 400 workers after a summer lay-off.

h: Marco Rubio visits Portugal on Thursday
t: The US secretary of state goes to Iceland and Greece first. He said Portugal has "again become a strong ally".

h: The attorney-general scraps the EU-funds anti-fraud group
t: Amadeu Guerra cites the end of the recovery plan, four public bodies pulling out and weak cooperation with the European Public Prosecutor. The DCIAP takes over and must map the riskiest areas by year end.

h: Parliament opens to visitors on the last Saturday of every month
t: Speaker José Pedro Aguiar-Branco announced it on the Republic's 116th anniversary. The first open Saturday is 31 October.

h: One gullible AI agent can pass an attack to every agent it talks to
t: In the past five months Google and four other organisations have acknowledged a flaw in how their AI agents talk to each other. Independent researcher Syed Anas Mohiuddin tested agents at Google, JPMorgan Chase, Weaviate, Rapid7, the French government's digital directorate and the US federal government. His proof-of-concept attacks use prompt injection against one special-purpose agent, say for translation or data analysis, rather than against the language model. Such agents often have weak guardrails or none, and they pass the instructions down the chain. Because agents connected over MCP, the Model Context Protocol, are built to trust each other, the next agent obeys, and MCP servers hold credentials for each agent. Attacks a model would refuse directly can then exfiltrate database contents.

h: The Pentagon has stopped using Anthropic's models
t: The BBC says the phase-out ordered after the spring dispute over surveillance and weapons limits is complete. Meta and Microsoft are reported to be restricting internal use, weeks before Anthropic's planned IPO.

h: GitHub Actions went down for more than two hours
t: From about 21:00 German time hosted runners failed with "not acquired by Runner of type hosted"; Pages and billing were hit too. GitHub gave the all-clear at 23:32, with a queue to clear.

h: Artificial (2026): Guadagnino's Sam Altman satire wins over its first audience
m: Tech satire · Neon · US cinemas 25 Dec
t: Luca Guadagnino's film premiered at the New York Film Festival on Monday, with Andrew Garfield as the OpenAI chief during his brief ousting in 2023. Simon Rich wrote it, Ike Barinholtz plays Elon Musk and Damon Albarn wrote the score. Amazon MGM greenlit it but dropped the finished film this year, soon after Amazon signed a $50 billion cloud deal with OpenAI. Neon picked it up and will release it in US cinemas on 25 December with an Oscar campaign. First reactions call it "savage" and "terrifying". No European date yet.

h: Emily Blunt returns for a third Sicario
m: Crime thriller · in development
t: She rejoins Josh Brolin and Benicio Del Toro. Padraic McKinley ("The Weight") directs from a script by Steven Knight.

h: Whitney staff ratify a contract hours before their strike
t: Unionised workers at the Whitney Museum ratified their second contract on Sunday night, hours before a strike set for Monday, three days before previews of the Roy Lichtenstein retrospective. Every employee gets at least 14.75% more over four years. The lowest-paid get 5% to 23% in the first year, and new-hire minimums go up. The deal adds longevity bonuses after ten years, up to 12 weeks of paid parental leave and more bereavement leave. The union, which represents nearly 200 staff, is part of the United Auto Workers.

h: Krasner and Pollock, side by side at the Met
t: Hyperallergic calls "Past Continuous" one of the best-installed shows in the museum's history and asks how Lee Krasner made her work, and survived, beside Pollock.

h: The PEOPLE festival is back in Berlin, with no line-up at all
m: Festival · Funkhaus Nalepastraße · this week
t: Nearly 200 musicians spend a week at the old East German radio centre on Nalepastraße making new music together, and nobody knows yet who will end up on stage with whom. The idea came in 2015 from a circle around Bon Iver, Aaron and Bryce Dessner of The National, and Nadine and Tom Michelberger. It is non-commercial, and it last ran in 2016 and 2018. This year Kings of Convenience, members of Arcade Fire, The National and Yeah Yeah Yeahs, and Leonard Cohen's son Adam are taking part. radioeins is reporting from inside.

h: Einstürzende Neubauten's Kollaps (1981) turns 45
m: Industrial · debut album
t: The Quietus revisits a record built from scrap in a ruined West Berlin. The band formed for a gig at the Moon Club on 1 April 1980, named on the spot by Blixa Bargeld.

h: Animals (2026): Ben Affleck directs and stars as a candidate whose son is kidnapped
m: Political crime thriller · R · 1h 46m · Netflix · 9 Oct
t: Affleck plays Milo Bradford, running for mayor of Los Angeles. When his son is taken, he and his wife must find a ransom when nearly all their money has gone into the campaign, and raising it drags them into a criminal underworld and exposes secrets they meant to keep. Gillian Anderson and Kerry Washington co-star. Affleck wrote the original script with Connor O. McIntyre and Billy Ray (Captain Phillips). It is the next film from Affleck and Matt Damon's Artists Equity for Netflix, after The Rip. Damon was first meant to play the lead but had to leave for Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey. It opens worldwide on Netflix on Friday, and in some cinemas. Reviews are under embargo, so there are no scores yet.

h: Lorne (2026): Morgan Neville's portrait of the SNL founder
m: Documentary · Netflix (US) · 5 Oct · IMDb 7.0 · RT 74%
t: In cinemas in the US in April, now on Netflix's US service. Tina Fey, Conan O'Brien, Maya Rudolph and Chris Rock talk about Lorne Michaels, who still gives little away.
s: What's on Netflix · IMDb · Rotten Tomatoes

h: Dead-End Job (2026) is a horror show of a workplace
m: Fantasy horror · 8 episodes · Netflix · 9 Oct
t: Lee Jae Wook plays a desperate man who takes a suspiciously well-paid job and finds himself in a supernatural, hellish office. Go Min Si co-stars.

h: Sánchez calls a snap election for 29 November
t: The call follows Friday's defeat of his housing measures, which the cabinet is now re-approving for a fresh vote in Congress. The CCOO and UGT unions plan a general strike over housing in October, date to be set.

h: Quebec separatists win power and promise a third independence vote
t: Canadian media project a minority win for the sovereigntist Parti Québécois in Monday's provincial election, its first time in power since 2014. Its leader, Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, becomes premier and has pledged a referendum on independence after Quebec's votes of 1980 and 1995, but only after Donald Trump leaves office, which would mean 2029 or 2030. Polls put support for leaving Canada at about 30%. He also promises to fight Ottawa on immigration. Prime Minister Mark Carney may face two unity crises at once: Alberta votes on separation later this month.

k: Brazil decides · Counted in Portugal too
h: Bolsonaro's son wins Brazil's first round, but Lisbon and Porto vote for Lula
t: Flávio Bolsonaro leads President Lula 47% to 45% and the two meet again on 25 October. A record 134,797 Brazilians registered to vote in Portugal, and in Lisbon and Porto they backed Lula by about fifteen points. With almost every ballot counted, Flávio Bolsonaro, 45, the eldest son of the jailed former president Jair Bolsonaro, had 47.03% of the vote to 45.16% for Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, 80, who is seeking a fourth term. Polls had shown Lula slightly ahead. Neither reached 50%, so they face a run-off on 25 October. Observador puts Lula's gap at about 2.3 million votes, his weakest first round since 2002. Turnout was 78.9% of more than 158 million registered voters. Bolsonaro's Liberal Party won 19 of the 54 Senate seats up for election. With nine senators already sitting, it will hold 28 of 81, the largest group. Michelle Bolsonaro was elected senator for Brasília with a record vote, and two of Jair's sons and his brother won seats as well. Flávio has promised an amnesty for his father, who is serving 27 years for plotting a coup, and for the rioters of 8 January 2023. In Portugal the count went the other way. In the Lisbon consular area, which had the most voters, Lula took 14,948 votes (53.51%) to Bolsonaro's 10,548 (37.76%). In Porto he won by 10,356 to 7,559. Only the small Faro consulate went to Bolsonaro, by 1,305 votes to 1,097. Lisbon had about 79,000 registered voters, Porto more than 47,000 and Faro close to 9,000. Portugal is the second-largest polling area outside Brazil, after the United States. Most of them stayed home. Voting is compulsory in Brazil for literate adults from 18 to 70, but abstention in Portugal reached 62%, against 21% in Brazil itself. Voters abroad choose only the president and vice-president, so they will be back at the polling stations on 25 October.
s: RTP · Lusa · TSE · Observador · BBC · 5 October

h: Ovar's half marathon breaks its entry record again, and Bernardo Rocha wins a third time
t: The 36th Meia Maratona Cidade de Ovar, organised by AFIS/Ovar on Sunday, had close to 5,000 entries, a record for the race. Bernardo Rocha of SC Salgueiros, who also won in 2023 and 2024, crossed the line first in 1:06:13. Francisco Rodrigues of Braga was six seconds behind and Vítor Oliveira (GDC Guilhovai) two minutes back. The women's race went to Rocha's clubmate Maria Vinagre in 1:15:14. Mónica Silva, winner of the last two editions, finished 1:26 behind her, and Joana Ferreira of Beira-Mar 2:42 behind. The 10 km Corrida do Azulejo grew even faster, from 746 finishers last year to 1,173. Simão Bastos won in 31:01 and Telma Pinho in 36:51.

h: More women are doing sex work along the forest road from Esmoriz to Furadouro
t: OvarNews reports the numbers rising along the road through Maceda and Cortegaça, and a former council official says police "can't do anything". Litter left in the pine woods is the most common complaint. The Esmoriz community centre's "Carrinha Dá a Volta" van has offered health care on the road every day for almost 20 years.

h: Ovarense open the league season by beating Braga 96–83
t: They led 52–28 at half-time in the Arena de Ovar, and Braga's late run (35–21 in the last quarter) came too late.

h: Three of the five new Crasto residences are still closed to students
t: The rector, Artur Silva, says the rest of the PRR-funded beds depend on "complementary works" being finished first.
s: Notícias de Aveiro · Rádio Universidade de Aveiro

h: The Left takes Katherina Reiche to the constitutional court
t: An urgent application targets a ministry Instagram video in which she called the Left, after its Berlin win, dangerous for the city. The party says it breaks the duty of neutrality. A deadline to take the video down passed on 29 September.

h: The new e-car grant has paid out to 100,000 buyers since May
t: Three in four have a taxable household income of €60,000 or less, says environment minister Carsten Schneider. Fewer than 15% of applications are for cars made in China.

h: New J-series trains run on the U9 from today
t: Two six-car sets to start with, between Rathaus Steglitz and Osloer Straße. 124 cars are now in service and 170 are due by the end of the year. On the U5, punctuality rose from 98.4% to 99%.

h: The Kältehilfe season has begun, and the city is short of buildings for it
t: Night shelters get up to €35 per bed per night, occupied or not. Leases are capped at seven months, though, and neighbours have blocked some sites.

h: Pepper spray attack on young Left members in their party office
t: Police are looking for three people. One asked beforehand whether you could "vote AfD here". It is the second attack on the office in a few weeks.

h: SPD members draw their red line on the working-hours reform: no weekly limit without a union deal
t: German law sets an eight-hour working day, longer only in exceptional cases. On page 18 of their coalition agreement, the Union and the SPD promised to allow a weekly maximum instead. The CDU and CSU want employers and staff to share out the hours within that week as they choose. Talks resume this week, and four of the SPD's largest member groups have now set out conditions in a seven-page paper titled "Self-determined, not deregulated". The SPD women, the labour working group, the Jusos and the "60plus" group all signed it. They accept a weekly limit only where a collective agreement covers it, a point they say no law may drop. Roughly half of German employees work under one. The paper wants an average cap of 40 hours a week and paid overtime premiums from the first extra hour. It asks for every employee's time to be recorded electronically, for working hours to be set only by mutual agreement, and for sectors prone to undeclared work to be left out. Labour minister Bärbel Bas tried almost the same union-deal rule in a draft in June and backed down after business groups and the CDU objected.

h: Nearly half the new cars sold in Portugal in September were battery-electric
t: Portugal sold 19,589 new passenger cars in September, 15.2% more than a year earlier, the car industry association ACAP reports. 47.7% of them ran on batteries alone. Observador puts much of the growth down to electric models and suggests that rising fuel prices played a part. Light commercial vehicles grew 4.7% and heavy vehicles 3.9%. From January to September, 188,912 passenger cars were sold, up 10.1%. Over the same period, light commercials rose 9.2% to 25,133 and heavy vehicles jumped 33.8% to 6,881.

h: Seguro opens Belém's gardens for the Republic's 116th birthday
t: The palace gardens and the Presidency Museum are open from 15:00 to 18:00. The president gives his first Republic Day speech at the Praça do Município.

h: Yellow warnings for thunder and heavy rain in nine districts
t: Hail has already fallen in places. The unsettled weather lasts until Wednesday.

h: Google blacked out its data centres' water use, but you could copy and paste it
t: Nebraska requires data centres to report their electricity and water use each year, and Google marked the figures for all three of its sites as trade secrets. But reporters at 10/11 NOW in Lincoln found the redaction boxes were only drawn on top of the text. Highlighting them and pasting into another document revealed the numbers. The Lincoln site ("Agate LLC") drew 52.65 MW at peak and used 13.3 million US gallons of water last year, about 50,000 m³. The Papillion site used 547.88 million gallons in 2025, about 2.1 million m³. Together, the six data centres that have reported so far used 765 million gallons. The hidden boxes also showed the 2025 tax refunds Google's three sites expect: $55.8m, $39.2m and $22.6m.

h: Hackers reportedly reached a supertanker's propulsion system
t: The FBI and the US Coast Guard boarded the fully loaded VL Prosperity in August after it went silent near Gibraltar. Bloomberg says investigators found intruders had access to its engines.

h: VW picks London's Wayve over Nvidia
t: Wayve won test drives in London traffic. Its software is one neural network, end to end, and needs no HD maps. Mercedes, Nissan and Stellantis work with Wayve too.

h: Digger (2026) opens to $8 million, the biggest flop of Tom Cruise's career
m: Satirical comedy drama · 2h 9m · Warner Bros. · IMDb 7.3 · RT 51%
t: Alejandro G. Iñárritu's satire, with Cruise as an oil tycoon, took $8 million in North America. Verity, the weekend's other new release, opened to $32.6 million, and holdovers Resident Evil and Primetime also beat it. Abroad it made $12 million from 74 markets, so the worldwide total is $20 million. The official budget was $125 million, though IndieWire's sources put it at $160–180 million. It needs roughly $300–350 million to break even and is heading for a loss of $150 million or more. That puts it with John Carter and The Lone Ranger. Cruise's last softer opening was Lions for Lambs in 2007, a $35 million film. The flop lands as David Ellison merges Warner Bros. with Paramount and replaces the auteur-friendly film chiefs who greenlit it.

h: The History of Concrete (2026) passes $1 million
m: Comedy documentary · 1h 41m · Magnolia · IMDb 7.7 · RT 97%
t: John Wilson's urbanism film, made "in the style of a Hallmark movie", is the year's top platform-release documentary after 16 days.

h: Switzerland pays its museums to find out where their collections came from
t: The Swiss Federal Office of Culture is putting $2.4 million into 26 provenance projects for 2027 and 2028, picked after a public call. The focus is on objects acquired in colonial, archaeological and Nazi-era contexts. Basel's Natural History Museum and Gadjah Mada University in Indonesia get $120,000 to trace 189 Indonesian human remains in the museum's collection, how they were acquired and which communities they may come from, as groundwork for talks about restitution. Nine museums, among them the Museum der Kulturen Basel and the Bern Historical Museum, share CHF 100,000 (about $120,000) to study more than 6,300 objects from Cameroon. The Kunstmuseum Basel will re-examine 336 drawings whose provenance has been flagged, along with what happened to their sellers and how the museum collected between 1933 and 1945.

h: MAAT turns ten, and is free to visit until today
t: More than three million people have visited Lisbon's riverside museum of art, architecture and technology since it opened.

h: Steve Reich turns 90, and the pop world still samples him
m: Minimalism · composer · 90 on 3 October
t: Reich and Philip Glass met at Juilliard in the late 1950s and founded minimalism, along with a New York removals firm, Chelsea Light Moving. Reich's reach goes far beyond concert halls. The Orb built "Little Fluffy Clouds" (1990) on his Electric Counterpoint, which led to the Reich Remixed album four years later. Madvillain sampled his tape piece "Come Out" for "America's Most Blunted", and Brian Eno credits Reich's early tape loops as an influence. The Quietus also lists Talking Heads, Aphex Twin, Jonny Greenwood and Max Richter as heirs. Its birthday piece picks ten records as ways into six decades of work.

h: David Sylvian's first proper album since 2009
m: Instrumental · improvisation · one 46-minute piece
t: The Distance Between the Killer and the Killing is built from sessions recorded between 2012 and 2025.

h: The Reluctant Vampire (2026): the Alan Partridge writers make a family comedy, and Lenny Rush steals it
m: Family comedy · 6 episodes · BBC (UK) · IMDb 6.4
t: Neil and Rob Gibbons, who write the recent Alan Partridge series, have adapted Eric Morecambe's 1982 children's book The Reluctant Vampire and its 1983 sequel, The Vampire's Revenge, as a six-part comedy for children that leaves in jokes for their parents. An undead, more or less royal family lives in a gothic castle. The father, Victor (Tom Davis), loves hunting humans, his wife Valeeta (Sian Clifford) gives off Morticia Addams energy, and their son Vernon (Gabriel Nagy, in his first big screen role) can name a blood vintage from a single sip. The title vampire is their other child, played by 17-year-old Lenny Rush. Bill Bailey, Ross Noble and Asim Chaudhry fill out the cast. The Guardian's Lucy Mangan calls it "an absolute joy" and "perfectly cast". It is a BBC show reviewed for UK viewers, and no Portuguese or German release has been announced.

h: Steel Ball Run: JoJo's Bizarre Adventure (2026) hits its stride
m: Animated action adventure · weekly episodes · Netflix · IMDb 9.4
t: It is 1890, and a millionaire stages a $50 million horse race across America. It stands alone from earlier JoJo seasons, and episodes two and three take the race into the Arizona desert.

h: Lanterns (2026) ends its first season quietly
m: Superhero crime drama · 8 episodes · HBO / HBO Max · IMDb 7.8 · RT 92%
t: Chris Mundy, Damon Lindelof and Tom King's finale puts character before spectacle, introduces a new Green Lantern oath and leaves the door open for a second season.

h: The US pulls all its bombers out of Fairford
t: About a dozen B-1s flew home on Sunday, eight days after the arrests near the base. Whitehall does not dispute that the incident is the reason; the Pentagon gave none.

h: Vice-chancellor Babler will step down as SPÖ leader
t: After two weeks of infighting he goes by the end of the year. Finance minister Markus Marterbauer is to become vice-chancellor once he has finished cancer treatment.

h: Tigray's rebels leave Mekelle, and government forces take the city
t: The Tigray People's Liberation Front, which has run the region, says it has withdrawn "temporarily" from the regional capital to spare civilians as the fighting moved closer. Two residents told the BBC that pro-government forces now control Mekelle, and that mobile phones work again in parts of the city. Fighting broke out in recent weeks across Tigray, Afar and Amhara. Last month the TPLF joined six other armed groups, including Amhara's Fano militia, in an alliance that aims to remove Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. On Sunday the presidents of Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia and Sudan met in El-Alamein and called for respect for states' territorial integrity. Ethiopia accuses Egypt, Eritrea and Sudan of backing the rebels, which they deny. The 2020–22 war, ended by the Pretoria Agreement, killed an estimated 600,000 people.

h: Merz arrives in Kyiv with thousands of interceptor drones and €1.35 billion
t: The chancellor came by special train on Sunday morning, a few hours after Russia warned foreign visitors and diplomats to get out of the Ukrainian capital. Friedrich Merz arrived in Kyiv on Sunday morning, unannounced, on a special train. With him are Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and ten executives from the arms and energy industries. Government sources say he will promise Ukraine's forces the early delivery of thousands of interceptor drones, built to bring down Russia's fast jet-powered attack drones, and push joint production of long-range weapons that can hit supply lines behind the front inside Russia. One billion euros from budget funds that are already approved is to be released for this, plus another €350 million to repair and rebuild destroyed power plants. The defence ministers of both countries are due to sign a letter of intent on buying long-range systems made in Ukraine. The timing is the point. Only hours before the train pulled in, Russia's foreign ministry told foreign visitors and diplomats to leave Kyiv and to stay away from military sites and government buildings. On Friday and Saturday Russian strikes hit three of the city's six road bridges and then the Pivnichnyi (Northern) Bridge. tagesschau calls it probably the most dangerous trip a chancellor has made to the war zone since 2022. "Soon the fifth winter of war begins," Merz said. "Russia is bombing cities, homes and heating plants." He came, he said, because Ukraine needs all its partners' support in the coming weeks, and he would tell President Zelensky: "You can keep counting on our help." Germany is Ukraine's biggest backer in money and arms, but resistance to the aid is growing at home. Days ago Foreign Minister Wadephul met Sergei Lavrov in New York; Lavrov said afterwards the talk brought nothing new.

h: Ovar sells 4.2 hectares of forest land so Alcobre can expand its cable plant
t: The council has approved, by a majority, a promissory contract to sell about 4.2 hectares of land under partial forest protection to Alcobre, the electrical-cable maker, for around €2 million. The company wants to enlarge its Ovar factory and needs the land before AICEP, the national investment agency, can give the project "potential national interest" (PIN) status. Alcobre has already asked the nature agency ICNF to take the plot out of the forest regime. In return, an area next to the Ovar dunes forest would be put under protection instead. PS and Chega councillors abstained. PS's Emanuel Oliveira called the deal very important for a company with a long history in the concelho, but said his party did not like being forced to choose between its fight for green space and local jobs. The municipal assembly still has to approve the contract.

h: Aveiro opens a call for a resident artist
t: The council approved an open call under the CreArt 3.0 network, with travel and lodging paid. This year's residency feeds the city's Christmas programme, Boas Festas em Aveiro.

h: The region's museums sign up to a shared charter
t: The first meeting of the Aveiro region's museum network opens the region's 37th-anniversary programme on 10 October at the Museu Marítimo de Ílhavo.

h: Murtosa parish centre ends its home-care service
t: The Centro Social Paroquial de Santa Maria da Murtosa will stop home help for older people by the end of the year, blaming steadily rising costs.

h: Left, Greens and SPD agree on "a common path" and want a result next week
t: Saturday's second round of pre-talks ended with identical statements. Agreement is the condition for formal exploratory talks; details stay confidential.

h: Steinmeier warns that extremists endanger unity itself
t: The president, who leaves office in March, said at the Bremen ceremony that forgetting 1989 "would be betrayal".

h: Polish firms move west: 19 now work in Brandenburg
t: Budimex is building four bridges in Berlin and Brandenburg, including a €34 million one over the Silokanal, with about 70% of the work going to German subcontractors.

h: Deutsche Bahn keeps its €99.99 family ticket for good
t: The summer-only offer becomes a permanent fare from 1 November: a return trip on long-distance trains for up to five family members costs €99.99, ICE seat reservations included. Sales start on 26 October. DB chief Evelyn Palla told Bild am Sonntag the reason is simple: during the summer holidays the railway carried 100,000 more families than a year earlier. Palla did not promise the same jump in punctuality. Much of the network has been neglected for years, she said, and is "too old, too prone to faults and fails too often". The system can only be renewed piece by piece, not caught up in one or two years.

h: The Court of Auditors threatens to take the government's reform to the Constitutional Court
t: Parliament is debating a rewrite of the law that organises the Tribunal de Contas, the body that checks how public money is spent and must clear big public contracts in advance. Its president, Filipa Urbano Calvão, says the court will not "leave the stage". In interviews on Saturday she said there are grounds to send parts of the reform to the Constitutional Court, and put pressure on President Seguro, who can ask that court to review a law before signing it. She says some of the new norms run against the law.

h: Ventura will chair the inquiry into ex-police chief Luís Neves
t: The commission will examine Neves's years as national director of the Polícia Judiciária, 2018 to 2026. The Chega leader promises impartiality.

h: Alcohol dependence has nearly quadrupled in ten years
t: Only about one in five people with the disorder is in treatment.

h: The man who wrote OpenAI's safety reports quits and calls its culture broken
t: David Robinson wrote the safety reports that came with every major OpenAI model release. He resigned this week and has set out his reasons in The Atlantic. The problem, he argues, goes deeper than any new rule on how models are trained: Silicon Valley builds ever bigger systems with "extreme confidence", "perpetual sprints" and an "unimpeded optimism" that plays down what could go wrong. AI companies, he writes, need humility and outside views. "The time for trial and error is over," he told Reuters. It follows OpenAI's own admissions this autumn that its agents misbehaved and that a model was scrapped over safety.

h: Milt Windler, the flight director who helped save Apollo 13, dies at 94
t: He led one of Mission Control's shifts during the 1970 crisis. “We were making history,” he later said.

h: A US judge calls a warrantless Flock search unconstitutional
t: Judge Sara Hill threw out evidence found after a deputy searched the licence-plate database, calling it "indiscriminate mass surveillance". The ruling sets no binding precedent.

h: Atonement (2026): a US soldier asks to meet the Iraqi family his platoon shot
m: War drama · 1h 58m · dir. Reed Van Dyk · US cinemas since 2 Oct · IMDb 6.9 · RT 89%
t: In Baghdad in 2003, the Kachadoorian family drove through an intersection during a firefight to reach their home around the corner. A Marine platoon took them for insurgents and opened fire, killing three of them. Years later Lu Lobello, one of the soldiers, asked the reporter Dexter Filkins to help him meet the survivors, who had moved to the United States. Filkins told the story in the New Yorker in 2012; Reed Van Dyk now makes it his first feature, with Boyd Holbrook and Kenneth Branagh. The Film Stage, reviewing it at Toronto, praises a harrowing opening act but finds the reconciliation half too restrained and too broadly anti-war to face the hard questions. It opened in US cinemas on 2 October.
s: The Film Stage · IMDb · Rotten Tomatoes

h: A Statement (2026): Tom McCarthy's climate meeting that goes nowhere
m: Seriocomedy · NYFF premiere
t: The Spotlight director gathers climate scholars for one long, futile summit in St. Petersburg, Florida. IndieWire finds it light entertainment that hardly rakes the muck.

h: New York doubles its grants for individual artists to $10,000
t: For almost 20 years, city-funded grants to individual artists in New York were capped at $5,000. On Friday Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the Department of Cultural Affairs doubled the ceiling to $10,000. “Artists are forced to make hard choices when it comes to living in this city and getting paid,” Mamdani said in a video in which he paints at an easel opposite the cultural affairs commissioner, Diya Vij. The money flows through borough arts councils, and most are taking applications now: Brooklyn until 11 October, the Bronx until 30 October, Manhattan until 12 November and Queens until 17 November; Staten Island opens in November. The city's culture department has a record $323.8 million for the 2027 fiscal year.

h: Ingrid Wiener, textile artist of the Viennese avant-garde, dies at 83
t: She worked across weaving, photography, painting and collage, and collaborated with Valie Export and Dieter Roth.

h: Who earns from AI songs, and who is left with nothing
t: Kai Noir makes deep-tech house and has a few thousand monthly listeners on Spotify, but he does not exist: he is an avatar from Daniel Troha, who says he runs Germany's first AI music label and makes his tracks mainly with Suno, then polishes vocals and adds guitars by hand. Suno reported two million paying subscribers at the start of 2026. The neo-soul singer Sienna Rose reached more than four million monthly Spotify listeners; Bayerischer Rundfunk's research suggests she is an AI project too, like the band The Velvet Sundown. Musicians fear for their incomes, since such systems are trained on their songs. GEMA is suing Suno for using known works without paying the people who wrote them.

h: Bowery Electric's Beat (1996), post-rock that kept the rhythm
m: Dream pop / post-rock · second album · 1996
t: Pitchfork revisits the New York duo's second album, a gauzy blend of shoegaze and beats that Simon Reynolds once filed under post-rock.

h: Get Jiro! (2026): Anthony Bourdain's sushi chef cuts his way through Los Angeles
m: Animated action thriller · adult animation · half-hour episodes · HBO Max, from 4 Oct (UK date) · IMDb 6.7 · RT 83%
t: In a near-future Los Angeles, every human desire can be had in virtual reality except food, so top chefs rule the city like crime lords and people kill for a reservation. Jiro, voiced by Brian Tee, is a taciturn sushi master and biker caught in a war between restaurants. The series adapts the graphic novel Anthony Bourdain wrote with Joel Rose. The Guardian calls it wild, pulpy and very gory, from a cheese grater to a crème brûlée blowtorch, but in on the joke, with real anger underneath about food as class currency. Not for the squeamish.

h: Marshals (2026): Kayce Dutton leaves the Yellowstone ranch
m: Neo-western crime drama · Paramount+, from 5 Oct (UK date) · IMDb 6.1 · RT 48%
t: Luke Grimes rides on as a lawman facing a hostage crisis. "As daft as ever," says the Guardian, but sure of its own mythology.

h: Schumacher '94: The Birth of a Legend (2026)
m: Sports documentary · 1h 45m · Netflix original, German · IMDb 7.4
t: A German Netflix documentary on the season that brought Michael Schumacher his first Formula One title. It is in What's on Netflix's list of this week's US arrivals.

h: Spain marches for housing after Congress rejects the decrees
t: More than 50 protests followed Congress's rejection of the emergency decrees. Organisers counted 500,000 in Madrid alone, the government 70,000. Talk of a snap election grows.

h: Brazil votes: Lula, 80, against another Bolsonaro
t: More than 158 million Brazilians are called to vote today in general elections. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva seeks re-election at 80; his main rival is Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the former president, who wants to return the bolsonarista camp to power. Polls put Lula ahead but point to a run-off. Relations with Washington hang over the vote: Brasília accuses the US of interference, refused an ambassador named without consultation, and saw its own ambassador's US visa revoked. Some 134,000 Brazilians are registered to vote in Portugal, most of them in Lisbon and Porto.

h: A Spandau recount hands the AfD a seat and shrinks Berlin's parliament by five
t: The AfD's Tommy Tabor, not the CDU's Bettina Meißner, won Spandau's first constituency, by 35 votes. The knock-on cuts the Abgeordnetenhaus from 158 seats to 153. The mistake was a single phone call. In one Spandau polling station the official record, the Niederschrift, was correct, but the quick result phoned through to the district election office was not. The routine check of the provisional result caught it, and a public recount of first votes on Thursday confirmed it: Bettina Meißner of the CDU, first declared the winner of Spandau constituency 1, is in fact 35 votes behind the AfD's Tommy Tabor. The district returning officer, Katrin Zickert, notes that the AfD also leads there on second votes. Because Berlin balances overhang seats with extra seats for the other parties, that one constituency moves the whole chamber. State returning officer Stephan Bröchler now expects 153 seats instead of the 158 announced on election night. The CDU, SPD and Greens each lose one, the Left two. Five people who had counted on a seat will not get one: Meißner, Martin Matz (SPD), Oda Hassepaß (Greens), and Coco Aglibut and Bettina Günter of the Left. The AfD stays on 29. The arithmetic of the coming government barely shifts. The Left, Greens and SPD, whose leaders began exploratory talks this week, would hold 91 of 153 seats, comfortably above the 77 needed. But Bröchler did have a warning for the parties: no one holds a mandate until the final result and the first sitting, and he called it "not a good procedure" that the CDU, SPD and AfD had already elected new group leaderships. The figures are not yet "set in stone", he said; the state election committee decides on 12 October. After a 2021 election so flawed it had to be rerun, he wants the next one to digitise the polling station record, recounts included.

h: The Museu de Aveiro closes on Tuesday for 18 months after all
t: The Museu de Santa Joana, Aveiro's main museum in the former convent of Jesus, shuts to the public from 6 October while €5.2 million of works go on. The council had promised it would stay open through most of the job, which began in July, but now says safety rules that out. The work covers the historic part of the building, the Igreja de Jesus and the old cloister, and is meant to cure rising damp, roof leaks, structural cracks and the rainwater drainage. It is expected to take 18 months, so the museum would reopen in spring 2028.
s: Observador · Diário de Aveiro · Central Press

h: A stolen jet ski turns up in a Cortegaça warehouse
t: Searches on 28–29 September found a jet ski taken in Paços de Brandão last December, a 1959 Ford and, next door, a Yamaha motorbike and a mini-moto.

h: Aveiro's new waste contract costs three times the old one
t: The eight-year tender has a base price of €36.2 million, against €11.2 million last time. Collection now costs €73.50 a tonne, up from €33.

h: No tap water in parts of Maceda on Wednesday morning
t: AdRA cuts supply on 7 October from 09:00 to 13:00 for network maintenance.

h: Hasso Plattner's foundation buys Potsdam's "Kreml" for €31 million
t: The empty former Landtag on the Brauhausberg becomes a campus for up to 6,000 law, social-science and economics students.

h: Berlin keeps its excellence title; Konstanz loses its
t: Freiburg, Jena, Cologne and two alliances join the list. FU, HU and TU Berlin stay in for 2027–2033.

h: 36 years on, few East Germans reach the top
t: The sociologist Michael Hartmann sees almost no progress and calls for quotas when top posts are filled.

h: Galeria files for insolvency for the fourth time in six years
t: Germany's last big department-store chain has asked the district court in Düsseldorf to open insolvency proceedings, after earlier filings in 2020, 2022 and 2024. Its 83 stores stay open for now; what happens to some 12,000 staff, and whether they get insolvency pay, is unclear. Galeria has belonged since summer 2024 to the US investor NRDC and a company of the businessman Bernd Beetz, and in July put 33 stores under review pending cheaper rents. The services union ver.di blames "hair-raising management mistakes" and owners who did not invest. Department stores' share of German retail has fallen from 4.2% in 2020 to 1.2%, according to the EHI institute; if Galeria goes, the classic Warenhaus goes with it.

h: Freedom-of-information reform would make citizens justify their requests
t: The coalition wants a "legitimate interest" test and to bar associations and media companies from asking. The former data commissioner Ulrich Kelber calls it democratically wrong.

h: Prosecutors open an inquiry into the US use of the Lajes base before the Iran war
t: The Ministério Público confirmed on Friday that it is investigating whether American forces used the Lajes air base on Terceira lawfully in the run-up to the US–Israeli offensive against Iran, which began on 28 February. The inquiry follows a complaint the Bloco de Esquerda filed in April, calling the use a "gross violation of international law". Foreign minister Paulo Rangel has denied any breach of the base agreement with Washington. Last week the Bloco delivered a letter with about 8,500 signatures to the prime minister's residence asking for the base to be closed to the bombing campaign.

h: Scope lifts Portugal to A+
t: The agency upgraded the republic from A on Friday and moved the outlook from positive to stable.

h: Montenegro signs a 17-country letter against cohesion cuts
t: For the EU's 2028–2034 budget, the leaders reject cuts to farm and cohesion funds and are open to new joint debt to pay for them.

h: Apple tightens Full Disk Access on the Mac because of AI agents
t: Apple says some developers use the macOS Full Disk Access permission in ways that expose "files, mail, messages, and even browsing history" without users understanding it, and that the risk will grow "substantially" as agents get more autonomous. New controls are meant to make the stakes clear before anyone grants it. The move follows the columnist Jason Aten's report that Meta's Muse agent quoted one of his Apple Messages threads unprompted. Meta's CTO said Muse can read Messages only with both Full Disk Access and its own connector switched on; the security researcher Patrick Wardle replied that Full Disk Access alone makes any non-root file readable. Apple named no app.

h: An AI finally beats the best Stratego player, on 16 GPUs
t: Ataraxos, from CMU, MIT, NYU and Stanford, beat Pim Niemeijer 15–1 with four draws after 163 million games against itself.

t: The crash-simulation solver, open-sourced by Altair in 2022, now has no public repositories; development moves to the paid Simcenter Radioss.

h: Behemoth! (2026): Tony Gilroy casts Pedro Pascal as a cellist in crisis
m: Drama · Searchlight, US cinemas 4 Dec · RT 84%
t: The Andor creator's return to the big screen is smaller and stranger than its title, says IndieWire: a character study of a session cellist in midlife crisis, played by Pascal in almost every scene and nearly without words. Its structure runs on music, as he records one Hollywood score after another and each session throws him back into memory. Gilroy hired nine composers, among them James Newton Howard, Michael Giacchino and Alan Silvestri, billed as The Behemoth! Collective, which may trouble the Academy's three-composer limit for Best Score. It was the New York Film Festival's centrepiece and opens in the US on 4 December.

h: Cameron Winter at Carnegie Hall (2026): Paul Thomas Anderson behind the camera
m: Concert documentary · NYFF
t: Anderson works his own Panavision camera onstage as the Geese frontman plays sparse piano versions of his songs.

h: Paramount plus Warner Bros. will be called Skydance
t: David Ellison names the merged studio after his old company. WB film chiefs Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy are out.

h: Bought for $30 at an estate sale, a Gertrude Abercrombie sells for a record $1.3 million
t: Alderman Merriam's Shells (1951) — nine small shells on a dark surface, a tenth hung on a black wall by an almost invisible thread — was picked up at a Michigan estate sale in June. Its anonymous buyer diverted a family holiday to see the touring Abercrombie retrospective at the Milwaukee Art Museum, found the painting reproduced in the catalogue, and had it confirmed by the scholar Susan Weininger. At Freeman's in New York on Thursday it was estimated at up to $200,000; the hammer fell at $1.3 million, beating the Chicago surrealist's previous record of $1 million.

h: Four New York museums settle with their unions
t: Staff at the Guggenheim, Brooklyn, Jewish and Folk Art museums ratify four-year deals; Folk Art workers get 13.6% over the term.

h: Elvis Costello's debut, unpacked into 104 tracks
m: New wave / pub rock · 1977 album · 5xCD 49th-anniversary box
t: My Aim Is True came out in 1977 when Costello was 22, and Pitchfork still calls it a masterpiece of "complaint-rock", with "Alison" its great soul ballad. The new five-disc set, issued with a wink on the 49th rather than the 50th anniversary, tries to explain where it came from. The second disc, The Blue Print, is the revelation: early demos and bedroom tapes from his pub-rock years with Flip City around London's Hope & Anchor, an ambitious writer steeped in Randy Newman, Warren Zevon and Lowell George. Later discs follow the change that came after Stiff's Jake Riviera suggested the name Elvis and the designer Barney Bubbles gave him a look.

h: Planet Opal in the studio
m: Electronic · krautrock-techno · Italian duo
t: Giorgio Assi and Leonardo De Franceschi have worked with Peter Hook and Berlin's Ellen Allien; their second album came out in 2025.

h: Africa: Earth's Wild Home (2026): a continent of cheetahs, frogs and flamingos on Disney+
m: Nature documentary series · Disney+, from 2 Oct
t: The new wildlife series from Disney goes habitat by habitat, from deserts to dense jungle, showing how each place shapes the animals that live there. IMDb credits the actor Wunmi Mosaku and the explorer Steve Boyes. The Guardian, which made it one of its seven picks this week, warns of a twee voiceover — at one point it imagines a dating profile for the black rain frog — but finds much of it spectacular: a cheetah hunting on a mountainside with his family's survival at stake is genuinely tense, and drone shots of a single hyena taking on thousands of flamingos are startling. It landed on 2 October; no critics' scores yet.

h: Until the Last Heartbeat (2021): a surgeon, his son and a mafia boss
m: Italian medical crime drama · Channel 4, 9 Oct (UK only) · catalogue
t: The 2021 Italian series Fino all'ultimo battito arrives in Britain: Marco Bocci's heart surgeon must choose between his sick son and a mob patient. "Emotionally overripe but gripping."

t: The 27-metre lava arch disappeared between 23 and 27 September, probably during Tropical Storm Nolo.

h: The G7 release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel, and Trump drops his export-ban threat
t: After a video call that included Chancellor Merz, the G7 agreed to put 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency stocks on the market over four months, under the International Energy Agency. That is roughly one day of world oil demand; who supplies how much is not yet known. The leaders also pledged no energy export restrictions among themselves, which binds the US too, and Donald Trump then said he would not ban diesel exports after all. Oil fell up to 5% in New York and Brent briefly dipped below $100. The Iran war has pushed OECD oil stocks to their lowest in 36 years.

h: Only one German in ten is satisfied with Merz's government, a record low
t: The October DeutschlandTrend has the government and the chancellor both at 10% approval, the worst ever recorded. The Union slips to 20% and the AfD stays clear at 27%. Just 10% of Germans are satisfied with the work of the federal government, and 10% with the chancellor's. Both are the lowest readings in the history of the ARD-DeutschlandTrend, which infratest dimap carried out among 1,303 voters from Monday to Wednesday. In the Sunday question the CDU/CSU loses a point to 20%. The Union has only once polled that low in the series, in September 2021. The AfD is unchanged at 27% and remains the strongest party. The SPD holds at 13%. The Greens gain a point to 16% and the Left loses one to 11%. The FDP stays at 4%, below the threshold. Together the two coalition parties now poll 33%. The mood behind the numbers is about money. Around half of those asked fear they cannot keep their standard of living. Asked how to fund the welfare state, 41% would accept higher contributions and 37% would rather see benefits cut; six in ten want any cuts staged by income. Only 17% trust the government to make the social systems secure. On energy, 74% say its measures do not go far enough. The fuel discount that started this week splits the country: 47% think it right, 46% wrong. The worries reach beyond the wallet. Two thirds fear people could lose control of artificial intelligence, the same share worries about Donald Trump's policies, and 54% fear Russia will attack further European countries. The biggest worry of all, at 84%, is that the parties find no common answers on the central questions.

h: Ovar's new police station gets the Court of Auditors' green light
t: The Tribunal de Contas has given its prior approval to the contract for the new PSP station in Ovar, the last step before building can start. The job was awarded for about €2.15 million, with 540 days to finish, and the station will go up on the former site of the municipal water and sanitation services. The same council meeting approved €249,341.91 for the carnival groups and samba schools, paid in advance because next year's Carnaval falls earlier than usual. It also revised rents in council-owned social housing from 1 November: each household's rent will be reset to its income and size, so some will pay more, some less.

t: Also listed: a €45,000 "Cooling Point" in Mauerpark and €760,000 of VeloFlow traffic-light displays for cyclists.

h: Görlitzer Park stays open at night after the Senate loses again in court
t: The Higher Administrative Court of Berlin-Brandenburg on Thursday rejected the Senate's appeal in the urgent proceedings over the night closure of Görlitzer Park. Like the lower court in June, it found the Senate's environment department had no authority to set opening hours: that power lay with the Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg district, and the law was only changed in July 2024, too late. The ruling cannot be challenged, though the main case is still to come. The CDU-SPD Senate decided on the closure in 2023 to curb drug dealing and violence and had 16 gates built around the park. Residents and the alliance "Görli zaunfrei!" brought the case. "A fence solves no problems, it at most moves them into the surrounding streets," said their lawyer, David Werdermann, who wants the new Senate to drop the plan for good.

h: A day of strikes: the civil service stops and easyJet cancels 443 flights
t: Three CGTP unions have called a 24-hour strike of general-career public servants for today, covering some 350,000 workers, with a demonstration. Schools, universities, courts, health services and council work such as rubbish collection may be hit. In the air, easyJet cabin crew begin a strike that runs until Tuesday, 6 October. The SNPVAC union says at least 443 flights from Lisbon, Porto and Faro are already cancelled. Separately, the freelance doctors who fill hospital rotas meet the health ministry again today, still waiting for the rule that sets their pay.

t: The Maritime Authority's five-month count also logs 2,609 first-aid cases.

h: Reddit will switch off its RSS feeds in November and its public API by March
t: Reddit's RSS feeds stop on 13 November 2026, and the public API follows by March 2027. The company blames scraping and abuse; the news came almost in passing, in an r/modnews post about tools for moderators, who are told to use a "Discord Relay" app instead. Reddit sells data licences to Google and OpenAI and is suing Anthropic and Perplexity for scraping, so AI firms that read Reddit through the API will now need a commercial contract. Social-listening and research tools lose access too. It is the next step after 2023, when API fees killed third-party apps such as Apollo.

h: Clarissa (2026) moves Mrs Dalloway to Lagos, and Neon sets it for December
m: Drama · 2h 5m · Neon, US 11 Dec · IMDb 6.3 · RT 95%
t: Arie and Chuko Esiri, the twin directors of Eyimofe, adapt Virginia Woolf across a single day in Lagos. Sophie Okonedo plays Clarissa, preparing a society party as old friends and lovers from her youth come back to her; in a parallel thread a young soldier, Septimus (Fortune Nwafor), is haunted by what he has seen. A highlight of this year's Directors' Fortnight in Cannes, it borrows the heightened melodrama of Nollywood the way Almodóvar and Todd Haynes borrowed from telenovelas and daytime TV, The Film Stage writes. Ayo Edebiri and David Oyelowo co-star. The first US trailer is out; the 11 December date is for the US.
