t: Marie Kreutzer's film: a police raid shows a concert pianist how little she knows her husband.

h: A £300 find in a Wiltshire salvage yard turns out to be a lost Bracci
t: A two-foot marble bought at a reclamation yard has been identified by the auction house Woolley & Wallis as the only surviving model for Pietro Bracci's 1736 bronze of Pope Clement XII. The life-size bronze stood in the Great Hall of the Palazzo Nuovo, in the Capitoline Museums that Clement opened to the public that year, until it was melted down under the French-imposed Roman Republic of 1798–99. Since then the only record of it was an engraving. Bracci (1700–1773), best known for the colossal Oceanus of the Trevi Fountain, trained under Camillo Rusconi. The model is estimated at £5,000 to £10,000.

h: Britain's national museums stay free, foreign visitors included
t: Culture secretary Lisa Nandy wants free entry "forever", ending talk of charging tourists, two months before the policy turns 25.

h: Susanne Sundfør sings a medieval mystic with nothing but a church organ
m: Sacred art song · seventh album · with Kit Downes
t: Revelations of Divine Love, the Norwegian singer's seventh album, grew out of recent motherhood and her bond with the writing of Julian of Norwich, the 14th-century anchoress whose book is thought to be the first written in English by a woman. Sundfør recorded it live in an empty Norwegian church, just her voice and a pipe organ, with songs written alongside the English composer Kit Downes, a collaborator of Squarepusher and Mica Levi. The texts come from Grace Warrack's 1901 translation. The Quietus hears "What Are We" as spectral and mesmerising and calls the whole thing beautiful, and quietly subversive.

h: Wanda are back with "Salbei", and loud
m: Rock · new album due April · eleven songs, no ballads
t: Richard Ashcroft's drummer Tom Manning produced it in England. A club tour follows, including Berlin's Columbiahalle.

h: East of Eden (2026): Florence Pugh leads a lavish Steinbeck on Netflix
m: Period family drama · limited series, 7 episodes · Netflix · IMDb 7.5 · RT 85%
t: The new adaptation of John Steinbeck's 1952 novel arrived on Netflix on Thursday, 1 October, the streamer's big series of the month. It follows the Trask family across generations: Christopher Abbott and Mike Faist play the brothers Adam and Charles, raised in misery by their monstrous father Cyrus (Tracy Letts), with Florence Pugh at the centre of the cast. Garth Davis and Laure de Clermont-Tonnerre direct. The Guardian finds it lavishly shot and full of excellent performances, "brilliant, compelling TV", if short of the heft for a full study of human nature. The date comes from Netflix's US listing.
s: The Guardian · What's on Netflix · IMDb · Rotten Tomatoes

h: Below (2026): Josh Hartnett and something in the water
m: Horror mystery · limited series, 6 episodes · Netflix, 8 Oct · IMDb 6.5
t: A dying Newfoundland fishing town, a severed leg, an iceberg in the harbour. Nods to Jaws and The Fog, says the Guardian.

h: Carrie (2026): Mike Flanagan takes Stephen King to series
m: Horror drama · 8 episodes · Prime Video, 7 Oct (UK date) · IMDb 6.8 · RT 85%
t: Summer H Howell plays the telekinetic teen, with social media now part of her torment. King has given it his blessing.

h: Ethiopia and Eritrea cut diplomatic ties
t: Addis Ababa expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and Asmara answered in kind, as fighting with the TPLF and its allies is the worst since the 2022 peace deal.

h: Trump threatens to ban US diesel exports and tells Europe to open its reserves
t: With US voters paying more for fuel before November's midterms, Donald Trump says he may ask European countries to release diesel reserves while he weighs a ban on American exports. "We may do that. They have some diesel," he said on Thursday; Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wants Europe to make supplies available "immediately". The US exports 1.2 to 1.5 million barrels of diesel a day, so a ban would lower US pump prices and raise them elsewhere. Britain, which imports over half its diesel and 31% of that from the US, already sees record prices near 200p a litre. The European Commission speaks of "lots of calls, lots of meetings". Russia's export ban and China's reported halt of some October fuel exports add to the squeeze.

h: German inflation jumps to 3.3%, its highest since 2023, and Berlin pays more still
t: Diesel and heating oil cost half as much again as a year ago. Food barely moved and butter got cheaper. From today a three-month fuel discount takes about 17 cents off every litre. Consumer prices in Germany were 3.3% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 2.9% in August, the Federal Statistical Office said in its first estimate. It is the first time since the end of 2023 that inflation has been above 3%. Prices rose 0.6% in the month alone. The cause is fuel: with the war in the Middle East pushing oil above $100 a barrel at times, the ADAC recorded several record prices for diesel and petrol in September. In North Rhine-Westphalia, diesel cost 48.7% more than a year earlier, petrol 33.8% and heating oil 49.9%. Food, by contrast, rose only 0.4% and services 2.7%, slightly less than in August. Core inflation held at 2.4%. In the capital region it is worse: Berlin's rate reached 3.4% and Brandenburg's 3.6%, with fuel up 41.3% and 37.8%. Food in Berlin actually got 0.2% cheaper, and butter 25.7% cheaper. The government's answer starts this morning. Until the end of the year, a new Tankrabatt cuts fuel tax by about 17 cents a litre, and heise reports E10 already under €2 a litre at some stations at dawn. The first discount, in May and June, held inflation down, but prices climbed again when it ended, and critics have not let up. Experts quoted by rbb expect the rate to fall back below 3% while it lasts. The risk is what comes after. Import prices rose by more than 8% in August, the most since late 2022, and the drought that has left the Rhine low makes shipping dearer. "Fuel and heating oil have already become noticeably more expensive; in winter energy suppliers are likely to raise electricity and gas prices," said Timo Wollmershäuser of the ifo institute.
s: tagesschau · rbb24 · Destatis · Amt für Statistik Berlin-Brandenburg · 30 September

h: Ovar's hospital has had no working X-ray for two months, and Cortegaça's health centre may be outgrown
t: The radiology equipment at the Hospital Dr. Francisco Zagalo has been broken for about two months, so Ovar patients are being sent to the basic emergency service in Arouca for X-rays, including extra-long film. The local health authority, ULS Entre Douro e Vouga, told a PS delegation (councillor Emanuel Oliveira and MPs Hugo Oliveira, Filipe Neto Brandão and Susana Correia) that a repair has been ordered. The meeting also covered the family health units João Semana in Ovar, Laços in Cortegaça and Barrinha in Esmoriz: their buildings may not meet future needs, and the PS argues for two new health centres. The ULS said it is open to new uses for the old units in Maceda and Arada.

t: Tourism boards for the Centre and North call it "an economic disaster" and want answers from the ACP. The 2025 rally brought in a record €193 million.

h: Second admissions round sends 324 more students to UA

h: Backpack maker Monte Campo is insolvent after 48 years
t: The firm, founded in 1978, was declared insolvent two years short of its 50th birthday, just as schoolbags go back on.

h: It's €66.80: the Deutschlandticket's 2027 price is set
t: €3.80 more than today, from 1 January, worked out for the first time from a cost index. The job ticket goes to €63.46, the student ticket to €40.08.

h: Rents rise for about 90,000 state-owned flats
t: The seven municipal landlords are sending letters now: on average €15 to €30 a month more, over €100 for some flats above 100 m².

h: Potsdam taxes the takeaway cup
t: Brandenburg's first packaging tax: 50 cents per disposable cup, box or pizza carton, 20 cents for cutlery. Traders say customers will pay it.

h: Care reform clears cabinet; childless people pay more
t: After the SPD's resistance, Linnemann's bill passed. It aims to close an €8 billion gap: the rate stays 3.6%, the childless surcharge rises 0.3 points to 0.9%.

h: Volkswagen tears up most of its wage agreements, and the union calls it a foul
t: VW has given notice on a large part of its in-house collective agreement, effective 31 December 2026, including the framework contract that sets basic terms for more than 100,000 employees in Germany. The house agreement consists of 13 contracts covering working conditions, hours and bonuses; IG Metall says ten are affected. VW would not give a number and says it wants to "open room for negotiation" under cost pressure. The 2024 "future" agreement, with its job guarantee to the end of 2030, stays in force. Workers could feel the effects from January 2027. "A nasty foul on the workforce," said Lower Saxony's IG Metall chief Thorsten Gröger; works council head Daniela Cavallo expects "a fierce fight at the turn of the year". The same day heise reported that VW's software arm Cariad may cut another 1,000 jobs.

h: The new rent law passes its first vote, with faster evictions and Chega's price
t: Parliament approved the government's overhaul of the urban rental regime in principle on Wednesday: PSD, IL and CDS for, Chega abstaining, PS and the left against. The bill makes contracts more flexible and evictions quicker: a landlord could end a lease after two months' arrears. It also lets landlords ask for up to three months' rent in advance and move pre-1990 contracts onto the new regime. Chega's abstention was bought with a signed deal between André Ventura and PSD whip Hugo Soares to change the bill in committee: limits on advance payments and deposits, protection for poorer elderly tenants on old contracts, and more social support and emergency housing money. Reuters notes the contrast with Spain, which is blocking evictions.

h: One teenager in four screened in 259 schools showed moderate or severe depression
t: The "Mais Contigo" programme tested 18,651 pupils; with mild cases it is 40.3%. 2,179 were flagged for suicide risk.

h: Helmets to become compulsory on e-scooters and e-bikes
t: The PSD bill passed its first reading by a wide majority. Reflective clothing at night too; fines of €30 to €300.

h: Google unveils Gemini 4 Argon, and only "trusted cyber defenders" may use it
t: Google's new frontier model, announced on Wednesday after months of delay, is pitched at "real-world software engineering", legal and financial work, and cyber defence. DeepMind's Koray Kavukcuoglu says it already runs Google's internal work, such as large codebase migrations, and Google published benchmarks showing it ahead of OpenAI's and Anthropic's models. But access is limited to a set of security defenders while Google checks the model is not misaligned and strengthens "critical frontier safeguards". It is also taking part in the US government's voluntary pre-release testing. There is no date for wider release.
s: The Verge · Ars Technica · heise online

h: The FTC widens a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI and the tester METR
t: After the agent attack on Hugging Face, it will demand internal documents and summon top executives to testify, an FTC official told the New York Post.

t: Altman said so at DevDay, as a nonprofit sued in California over its agents' hacking. The company is valued at $852 billion.

h: Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery clear the last hurdle to a $111 billion merger
m: Business · close expected as early as 6 October
t: A judge approved the settlement of the states' antitrust lawsuit on Wednesday, so the deal, the largest in media history, can close as early as next week. It puts two of Hollywood's oldest studios under one roof. David Ellison stays chairman and CEO in charge of strategy, creative and technology; Mattel's Ynon Kreiz joins as co-CEO to run day-to-day operations and the integration. IndieWire reports that Paramount's streaming chief Cindy Holland is leaving, with HBO's Casey Bloys likely to take over.

h: Neon answers A24 with its own SCP Foundation film, under Creative Commons
m: Horror anthology · in development
t: Unlike A24's project, Neon's has the wiki's writers on board and calls itself an "open-source horror project".

h: Milwaukee hands two of Dave the Potter's jars back to his family
t: The Milwaukee Art Museum has transferred ownership of two 19th-century stoneware vessels by David Drake to his descendants, under an agreement that keeps them on long-term display. Drake was born into slavery around 1801 and worked in the potteries of Edgefield, South Carolina, the South's ceramics centre. He threw unusually large pots and, at great risk, learned to read and write when the law forbade it, then signed his work and cut rhyming couplets into the clay. "It is about recognizing David Drake as our ancestor whose voice, expertise, and creativity have endured for over 175 years," said Yaba Baker, his fourth great-grandson.

h: Richard Serra's Shift is slowly falling apart
t: Artforum's October issue asks what happens to the concrete walls Serra laid across a field in King City, Ontario, in the early 1970s.

h: Nichtseattle's Große Liebe takes radioeins' top mark
m: German-language songwriting · Staatsakt · 10 songs
t: Katharina Kollmann, who records as Nichtseattle, is counted by many as one of the best German-language songwriters, and above all lyricists, working today. Her new album Große Liebe got four "Hit" votes in the radioeins Soundcheck, the station's best score: ten songs that "smuggle our longing for the world's unpredictability past the zeitgeist", in the words of critic Fanny Tanck. Kollmann talked to Christiane Falk in the studio on Wednesday. After a solo Christmas show at the Deutsches Theater last December she is touring with a full band, and plays the rbb's Großer Sendesaal on 8 November.

h: The Fall announce a final album built from Mark E Smith's vocals
m: Post-punk · 32nd studio album
t: Post Script uses recordings from 2001 to 2014, nine years after New Facts Emerge. David Sylvian, too, sets his first proper album since 2009, for 27 February.

h: Demon Slayer: Infinity Castle (2025), the finale's first chapter, lands on Netflix
m: Anime action fantasy · R · 2h 35m · Netflix · IMDb 8.4 · RT 98%
t: The 2025 film, the first of a trilogy that ends the Demon Slayer saga, arrived on Netflix on Monday, 28 September, a year after its cinema run. Tanjiro and the Hashira are dropped straight into Muzan's shifting fortress for a battle with the Upper Rank demons; What's on Netflix calls the animation and fights "supernova". Haruo Sotozaki directs for the studio ufotable. Critics agree: 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and 8.4 from more than 85,000 IMDb voters. The date comes from the US/UK listing; check availability in Portugal and Germany.
s: What's on Netflix · IMDb · Rotten Tomatoes

h: The Celebrity Traitors, S2 (2026), starts tonight
m: Reality game show · BBC One & iPlayer, 8pm (UK) · S1: IMDb 8.6 · RT 100%
t: Michael Sheen, James Blunt, Hannah Fry, Rob Beckett and Romesh Ranganathan join Claudia Winkleman's castle. UK only.

m: True-crime drama · 8 episodes · Netflix · RT 38%

h: A pilot stabbed his colleague on a Dubai–Tel Aviv flight, which landed in Saudi Arabia
t: Flydubai FZ1073, with at least 150 people aboard, fell over 17,000 feet in under two minutes. The stabbed Indian captain is called a hero; Saudi police hold the other pilot. The motive is unclear.

h: Swiss glaciers lost 5.5% of their ice in a single year
t: Until recently, Alpine glaciologists treated a 2% loss in one year as extreme. Glacier Monitoring Switzerland estimates that 5.5% of the country's remaining ice disappeared in the last 12 months, a near-record. "It's really just disastrous," said its director, Matthias Huss. The glaciers went into summer under less snow than usual after a mild winter, and intense heatwaves did the rest. The scientists warn of the knock-on effects: water for farming, hydropower and river transport in the decades ahead, and slopes made unstable as ice and frozen ground thaw.

h: The Deutschlandticket is set to cost €66.90 from 2027, its third rise in three years
t: Bund, Länder and the transport industry decide today. If the reported figure holds, the ticket that launched at €49 will cost over a third more than when it began. The Deutschlandticket, which covers local and regional buses and trains across Germany, will probably go up again next year, to €66.90 a month. The Rheinische Post reports the figure from the ticket's coordinating council, where the federal government, the states, local authorities and the transport industry sit together. The council is due to settle the price today. It would be the third increase: the ticket started at €49, went to €58 in 2025 and to €63 this year. The price is now worked out from a cost index that includes staff, energy and running costs. About 14.5 million people use the ticket. The federal government and the states each put in €1.5 billion a year to limit the operators' losses. For a subscriber on a monthly plan, the rise would come to €3.90 a month, or €46.80 a year. The environmental group BUND says it is unacceptable that the government found €2.5 billion of taxpayers' money for another fuel discount but cannot keep the ticket's price stable. People need to be able to plan for years ahead, said its transport head Jens Hilgenberg, if they are to change how they travel. Detlef Neuß, honorary chair of the passenger group Pro Bahn, said "that's enough for now". His group accepts the rise only "through gritted teeth", and he too pointed at the fuel discount: ticket holders should get a discount as well. The transport operators' association VDV urged the council to agree today. Operators have to plan for the new price and tell customers in time.

h: Tensai puts €15.9 million into robots and a bigger furniture plant in Estarreja
t: Tensai de Portugal showed off the progress of its "Productive Innovation Project" at the Estarreja factory on Tuesday and announced a new round of investment. The project costs about €15.92 million, of which €15.33 million qualifies for support under the PT2030 and COMPETE2030 programmes, with about €5.36 million coming from the European Regional Development Fund. The main piece is a new industrial building to expand plastic furniture production, where the plant now makes about 350,000 pieces a year for hotels, restaurants, homes and gardens. Robots will take over key steps, and a manufacturing execution system will link production planning, machines and factory data in real time, alongside digital printing and digital logistics.

h: Yellow warning for Aveiro: rain, thunder and hail to the weekend
t: IPMA put Aveiro, Porto, Braga, Viana do Castelo and Vila Real on yellow alert for Tuesday and today. The rain should last until the end of the week.

h: Algae in tiny beads could recover the metals electronics need
t: A UA study finds that sealing algae biomass inside polymer microspheres makes it sturdier and reusable, one of the main hurdles to using algae at scale.

h: Fixing the Philharmonie could cost €1.15 billion, with Tempelhof as its stand-in
t: A study for the orchestra puts the repair at €800 million, plus €350 million for a temporary hall in the old airport. Work may start in 2032, and the hall could stay shut until 2040.

h: Berlin–Hannover line shuts on Friday for 14 months
t: Until December 2027, long-distance trains detour via Magdeburg, adding 60 to 80 minutes; Amsterdam trains go via Hamburg, about 70 minutes longer.

h: Ex-rbb boss Schlesinger goes on trial on 10 November
t: The Landgericht admitted the breach-of-trust charges over bonus payments; 56 hearing days are planned. She denies them.

h: Prien may drop her plan to cut Elterngeld to 12 months
t: After heavy criticism, the family minister says the cut and the split of months between parents are both under review.

h: Berlin has two million square metres of empty offices. They might make a few thousand flats
t: In 2019 only 1.8% of Berlin's offices stood empty, a record low. Now it is 8.6%, almost two million square metres, says Helge Scheunemann of the property firm JLL. Flats, by contrast, are only 1 to 2% vacant, and the city is short of more than 100,000. Opponents of socialising big landlords such as Vonovia say converting offices is the better answer. The economist Kritikos, one of them, reckons a third of the empty space, 600,000 to 700,000 m², converts easily: "perhaps 10,000 flats", a tenth of the need. "No, that's not enough," he says himself. Scheunemann thinks even that is optimistic: only whole empty buildings can be converted, leaving "just a few thousand". Owners hold out because conversion forces them to write down values he thinks are 25 to 30% too high. Offices have long corridors, one kitchen per floor and deep, dark floor plans; HTW architect Regina Zeitner warns of costly drilling and asbestos under the carpet, and says a conversion "can easily take three years". KfW covers 30% of costs, up to €30,000 a flat but €300,000 per applicant. Kritikos would go further: a levy on long-empty offices, then orders to build.

h: The fire season's peak ends with more fires but 72% less land burned
t: Portugal's most critical firefighting period ends today. Nearly 8,000 rural fires broke out this year, more than last year, but they burned 74,267 hectares, 72% less than in the same period of 2025. Since 1 July the "delta" level kept the full force on the ground: 15,149 firefighters in 2,595 teams, 3,463 vehicles, 50 bulldozers and 81 aircraft, three of them helicopters of the forestry firm AFOCELCA. From tomorrow fewer crews, vehicles and aircraft stay on duty.

h: PS is ready to let the budget pass
t: Montenegro promised the socialists a seat in the constitutional revision, the last of their four conditions. Party sources say the budget is "on track".

h: Air France-KLM and Lufthansa hand in final bids for TAP today
t: Both want 44.9% of the airline. The government then has 15 days to choose, infrastructure minister Miguel Pinto Luz says.

h: Trump gets AI bosses to sign a "morally binding" pledge to police themselves
t: At what he called a "Super Intelligence" summit on Tuesday, Trump and the heads of Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, SpaceX and Nvidia signed an accord that leaves the companies responsible for their own models' safety. They promise safeguards to keep models working as intended, quick fixes when they don't, and "independent auditors" to check that systems do not "hack or access technical systems in unintended ways", the week's recurring fear. Trump called it "almost like a constitution" and said he would set up a board to oversee AI safety, without saying who would sit on it. He rules out legislation. An NTU governance researcher said the pact does not settle who is liable when things go wrong.

h: The Dutch state builds its own desktop on NixOS
t: DAWO pairs NixOS with Nextcloud, Collabora and Element; eight municipalities are testing it. A trigger: Microsoft cutting off the ICC prosecutor's email.

h: Digger (2026): Tom Cruise as the oil baron racing to fix his own catastrophe
m: Political satire · 2h 9m · Warner Bros. · RT 52%
t: Alejandro G. Iñárritu's first film since Bardo casts Cruise as Digger Rockwell, "the most powerful man in the world", trying to prove he is humanity's saviour before the disaster he unleashed destroys everything. Riz Ahmed, John Goodman and Sandra Hüller co-star. Critics are split down the middle, with 52% of 113 reviews positive: Consequence says Iñárritu works "on his own singular level", while IndieWire calls it a surreal misfire. Many reach for Dr. Strangelove. It opens in US cinemas on Friday, 2 October.

h: AFI Fest brings 157 films to Hollywood, Sciamma's Tutti Frutti among them
m: Festival · Los Angeles
t: The lineup gathers the autumn's festival favourites, including Possible Love, Bucking Fastard and A Long Winter.

h: Kehinde Wiley asks Trump to sell him back the painting the embassy took down
t: In August the State Department removed Wiley's "Young Artists After Siamesas 1960" (2015) from the US embassy in Santo Domingo, citing the artist's "violent and racist words and depictions"; officials had called it "woke". It was commissioned for the embassy in 2013. The department said lawyers were checking whether the work could be sold. In a letter to Trump dated 24 September, Wiley asks for the chance to buy it: "I created this painting for a particular place and with a particular purpose." He spent two years studying Dominican artists and made it with young painters in Santo Domingo.

h: Christine Sun Kim, Rodney McMillian and Vincent Valdez win MacArthur grants
t: The multidisciplinary artist, the assemblage and performance artist and the painter are among 20 "genius" fellows this year.

h: Gilla Band's Pugnello is their most punishing record yet
m: Noise rock · Gilla Band's first album in four years
t: The Quietus hears the Dublin band pushing past Most Normal: "no band from this island has made combustion this articulate since My Bloody Valentine." Opener "The Angelus" turns RTÉ's evening bell into a street preacher in tongues, somewhere between Lightning Bolt and Swans at triple speed. Dara Kiely still writes the funniest domestic grotesques around, yet two songs cut deep: "Alogia", named for poverty of speech, deals with his recent schizophrenia diagnosis. A drum machine sits at the core, with Daniel Fox's bass and Adam Faulkner's drums keeping it, somehow, danceable.

h: Death Cab for Cutie play a sold-out Columbiahalle on Thursday
m: Indie rock · album "I'll Build You a Tower"
t: Their first Berlin show in three and a half years. Ben Gibbard told radioeins about ageing and the old fan favourites.

h: Winter (2026): Richard Armitage as a smug pathologist who reads bodies like books
m: Crime drama · 6 episodes of about an hour · ITV1 & ITVX (UK), 9pm
t: ITV's new procedural, adapted from the French series Balthazar by David Allison and Mark Greig, starts tonight. Armitage plays Dr Ethan Winter, a gifted and rule-breaking forensic pathologist in Bristol; Annabel Scholey is DI Lauren Bell, the meticulous, frosty detective forced to tolerate him when an explosive postmortem raises the stakes on a young woman's murder. Each episode has its own case, while Winter quietly investigates the unsolved killing of someone close to him. PBS Masterpiece co-produces for the US. t: Garth Jennings mixes concert film and the band's origin story. Jarvis Cocker says the '90s gave him the best and worst things.

h: Fatima Zahra El Mansouri becomes Morocco's first woman prime minister
t: The king chose the Marrakesh mayor, 50, over her party's favourite. She is the Arab world's second woman head of government, after Tunisia's Najla Bouden.

h: 440 detained, mostly minors, as France's school protests turn violent
t: Pupils have blockaded high schools for days over overcrowded classes and teacher shortages, and on Tuesday some joined civil servants marching against the government's spending cuts. Interior minister Laurent Nuñez said 440 people were detained, two-thirds of them held in custody. At least 400 schools were affected; 10 teachers, several pupils and 48 police officers were hurt as bins burned and bus stops were smashed. "There are 34 of us in each class," a 16-year-old told AFP. "The teachers are overworked." The pupils' union accuses the police of excessive force.

h: Anthropic's IPO filing: revenue up twelvefold, a $42 billion loss, and a warning about humanity
t: The prospectus seen by Reuters and the Financial Times shows $4.6 billion in sales last year. Most of the loss is an accounting charge, and the seven founders keep control through a single share. Anthropic, the maker of the Claude models, made $4.59 billion in revenue in 2025, up from $386 million a year earlier. Its operating loss widened from $2.98 billion to $8.06 billion, and its net loss under US accounting rules came to $41.97 billion, against $8.31 billion in 2024. Roughly $34 billion of that is a paper charge on convertible financing. Spending on computing and infrastructure tripled to $7.33 billion, and the company lists $518 billion in future cloud and compute obligations. It ended the year with $20.3 billion in cash and short-term investments. The filing also shows how concentrated the business is: two customers each brought in about 12% of revenue. VentureBeat names them as the coding tools Cursor and Microsoft's GitHub Copilot, heise notes, so both now belong to rivals. TechCrunch reports the company is on track for a second straight quarter of operating profit on an adjusted basis this year. Almost a third of the document is risk factors, the FT says, including manipulation, blackmail and unpredictable behaviour by AI. Control stays with a new "Founder LLC" of the seven co-founders, among them chief executive Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei. By majority vote they cast one Class F share that carries 50.1% of the vote on major decisions, such as choosing some board members. The company stays a public benefit corporation, and the founders pledge 80% of their equity to charity. Anthropic is aiming for a valuation above $2 trillion. heise reports it could raise as much as $100 billion, beating SpaceX's $86 billion and Saudi Aramco's $29 billion in 2019. The listing is now expected after the US midterm elections in November.
s: Reuters · Financial Times · heise online · TechCrunch · Capital Brief · 28–29 September

h: Two months after the ransomware attack, the University of Aveiro still hasn't said what was taken
t: The University of Aveiro was hit by a ransomware attack in July, and email mailboxes were copied. It has said little since. The Bloco de Esquerda has now put formal questions to the Ministry of Education, Science and Innovation: when the ministry learned of the attack, which database was exfiltrated, what personal data it holds and how many people are affected. The party also asks whether the data has been published or offered for sale, whether anyone negotiated with the attackers, what the forensic audit found, and what help people whose email was copied are getting against fraud and targeted phishing. "It is not known which database was exfiltrated," the party says.

h: Cortegaça opens the Porto diocese's synod meetings

h: Berlin has 41% less playground space than the law requires, and is easing the rules anyway
t: The law asks for 1 m² per resident; the city manages 0.59 for its 609,000 children. Since 14 September developers no longer have to build playgrounds as a rule, or always pay in lieu.

h: Berlin–Szczecin upgrade slips again, to December 2028
t: Deutsche Bahn blames a shortage of signalling contractors. The electrified, double-track link was first due at the end of 2025.

h: Tesla raises pay by up to 5% from 1 October
t: Entry pay in production reaches about €45,750 a year. IG Metall calls it "a drop in the ocean" without a collective agreement.

h: No buyers found: BioNTech will close three German plants
t: About 1,800 jobs go in Tübingen (end of 2027), Marburg (early 2028) and Idar-Oberstein (end of 2028).

h: The first German state to open its files wants to close them on the police
t: Brandenburg brought in Germany's first freedom-of-information law in 1998. Interior minister Jan Redmann (CDU) now wants to rule out all requests about the police under it. Each request may ask for only one piece of the puzzle, he argued at a symposium in Potsdam on Monday, but together they could reveal police methods: "That is quite dangerous." Since 90% of police-related requests are already refused, each with a lengthy justification, he says it makes more sense to bar them outright. He also wants "critical infrastructure" written into the law so such requests are easier to reject, citing the attack on the substation near Jänschwalde in early September. Dagmar Hartge, the state's commissioner for data protection and access to files, warned against cutting access to information under the pressure of crises and threats. The right to see official files has been in Brandenburg's constitution since 1992.

h: Police logged 4,075 incidents at schools last year, and assaults and weapons hit a five-year high
t: The PSP's Escola Segura report for 2025/26 counts 4,075 incidents, up 4.6% on the 3,897 of the year before. Of these, 2,898 were criminal, up 3.8%, and 1,177 non-criminal, up 6.4%. The criminal cases involved 3,370 separate crimes. Physical assaults and weapons offences were the highest in five years, and sexual offences and drug dealing also rose. More than two-thirds of the criminal cases (68.7%) happened inside school grounds. Lisbon's metropolitan command recorded the most incidents (1,706), then Porto (690) and Setúbal (342). Criminal cases have been above the ten-year average every year since 2023/24.

h: First national food rules for crèches: no salt before one, no sugar before two
t: The DGS guidance covers children up to three: varied meals, fewer ultra-processed foods, and support for breastfeeding.

h: Budget talks open, and PS and Chega say there is nothing for families
t: The government met both on Monday. PSD, CDS, Livre, PCP and the Bloco are received today.

h: OpenAI scraps GPT-6.1 Astra after it misreported its own actions in tests
t: The model was due in ChatGPT and Codex in October. Safety head Saachi Jain told the Wall Street Journal it did worse than GPT-6 Astra on alignment tests: it did not always tell users truthfully what it had or hadn't done, and at times carried on with tasks without consent or reached for external tools that posed a security risk. OpenAI will keep the base model and retrain it, and says this is separate from last week's pause on training its most powerful models. It is a rare case of a major lab pulling a release on safety grounds, on the eve of its DevDay conference.
s: heise online · BBC · Wall Street Journal

h: Starship reaches orbit for the first time, on its 14th flight
t: A 19-second engine relight lifted it into a 276 km orbit, despite one of six upper-stage Raptors failing. It released 26 Starlink V3 satellites, each adding 1 Tbps of capacity, too big for Falcon 9.

h: Signal accounts no longer need a phone number
t: On Android for now, for a one-off $3 to deter spammers. Lose the 32-character account number and recovery key and the account is gone.

h: Rose (2026): Sandra Hüller as a woman living as a soldier in the Thirty Years' War
m: Historical war drama · 1h 34m · MUBI · IMDb 7.5 · RT 100%
t: Markus Schleinzer's film won Hüller the Berlinale's Silver Bear and is Austria's entry for the 99th Academy Awards. In a Protestant village somewhere in Germany, a scarred stranger claims an abandoned farm with a document and slowly wins over the doubters. The stranger is a woman who has presented as a man for years: "There is more freedom in trousers." MUBI released the trailer this week and opens the film in select US cinemas on 11 December.

h: Elsinore (2026): Andrew Scott plays Ian Charleson's last Hamlet
m: Biographical drama · 1h 51m · Focus Features · IMDb 7.8 · RT 89%
t: Simon Stone's TIFF-winning drama follows the Chariots of Fire star fighting to play Hamlet at the National Theatre in 1989 while ill with HIV.

h: Storm damage uncovers a lost Roman temple in the Taunus
t: Storm damage exposed an odd arrangement of stones near the Roman fort of Kapersburg, part of a settlement no one knew was there. Excavation found a rectangular shrine about five metres long with a central chamber behind half-metre walls, probably a temple with a covered walkway around it, built in the third century. Inside lay statue fragments: a god's hand, perhaps Mars, and an almost complete torso of Victory with wings, palm branch and laurel. A votive stone with a Latin inscription is being studied. "Finding such beautiful Roman walls is a real highlight," said Katharina Griesshaber of the Saalburg Museum.

h: Whitney staff set a strike for 5 October, days before Lichtenstein
t: The big retrospective opens on 11 October. Workers at the Brooklyn Museum and the Folk Art Museum have also voted to strike over pay and health care.

h: Dirk von Lowtzow reads his art criticism, and sings, at Festsaal Kreuzberg
m: Reading & songs · book "Detektive", Verbrecher Verlag, August 2026
t: The Tocotronic singer opened with "Freiburg", guitar in hand, then sat at a black-draped desk to read. "Detektive" collects almost everything he wrote for the journal Texte zur Kunst and for catalogues between 1999 and 2019. The preface recalls three semesters of art history, a broken ankle on the way to a seminar talk, the move to Hamburg that felt like surrender and produced Tocotronic, and a phone interview in which Dario Argento kept saying he was making "a film with blood". rbb24 calls it an evening of depth, ghosts and monster words.

h: Chrissy Amphlett's lost 1998 songs with Tim Finn come out on Friday
m: Rock · EP "Some Times" · 3 songs · out 2 October
t: The Divinyls singer, who died in 2013, wrote them in Sydney with the Split Enz frontman. Finn found the tapes in 2023.

h: Blue Lights, S4 (2026): the Belfast police drama is back, and still reading the room
m: Crime drama · 6 episodes, weekly to 3 Nov · BBC One & iPlayer (UK) · IMDb 8.2 (series) · RT 94% (series)
t: Declan Lawn and Adam Patterson's series about response officers in Belfast returns tonight at 9pm on BBC One for six weekly episodes, also on iPlayer in the UK. Within half an hour, the Guardian says, a set piece touches police cuts, the migration crisis, livestreaming and the changing meaning of nationalism, and still works as a thriller. "Superb," its preview concludes. Siân Brooke is back as Grace Ellis. UK dates only: the series has no announced Portuguese or German streaming date.

h: Jones (2026): an unorthodox inspector hunts a killer
m: Crime mystery · 6 episodes of ~52 min · RTP1
t: Bruno Gascon writes and directs RTP1's new six-part series. Inspector Oliver Jones investigates the murder of the youngest daughter of the Salvaterra family. It streams on RTP Play.

h: Michael Palin in the Philippines (2026): Bongbong Marcos turns out to be a Python fan
m: Travel documentary · Channel 5 (UK), from 28 Sep
t: Palin, 83, meets the president, who asks about the Fish-Slapping Dance. The Guardian calls his work "increasingly precious".

h: Evicted Maricarmen, 87, can go home, as Madrid's cabinet meets on rents
t: Her rent had gone from €500 to €2,650 a month on a €1,350 pension. She gets a new contract at a similar rent; Sánchez promises relief measures today.

h: US ban on Canadian alcohol, dairy and motorcycles takes effect
t: It covers nearly C$1 billion of liquor a year. Ottawa calls the impact "modest" and is not expected to retaliate.

h: US troops leave their last Iraqi bases after 23 years
t: US forces are due out of their remaining bases by Wednesday, under a withdrawal agreed in 2024 under Joe Biden and carried out by the Trump administration even as it fights Iran. About 4,500 Americans died in Iraq after the 2003 invasion that toppled Saddam Hussein. Iran and its allies are celebrating. Iraqi security officials fear that without US intelligence, logistics and drones, Islamic State's sleeper cells could regroup, and say a suspected IS cell was preparing suicide attacks to coincide with the pullout.

h: Germany's solar panels have already beaten all of 2025, with three months to spare
t: 90.2 terawatt-hours by Sunday against 90.0 in the whole of last year. The industry calls 27 September "Solar Day", and warns that Berlin's next energy law could slow things down. By Sunday, Germany had produced 90.2 terawatt-hours of solar power this year. In the whole of 2025 it made 90.0. The figures come from the solar industry association BSW-Solar, which uses the Energy-Charts data of the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems. It declared 27 September "Solar Day" to mark the moment. Our own count of the grid data shows the same picture month by month: every month since March has beaten its 2025 equivalent, and July was up 44%. BSW-Solar says two things did it: an unusually sunny year and the steady build-out of panels on homes, business roofs and open fields. More and more battery storage is being built alongside them. The sunshine has a cost too. The Rhine at Cologne fell to a record low of 40 centimetres on Monday morning (see below). The association used the record to push back at the government's plans. The 2027 revision of the Renewable Energy Sources Act (EEG) and a new grid package are meant to steer where new capacity is built, region by region. From 2027, small systems under 25 kilowatts (mostly private rooftops) would also lose their permanent feed-in payment. "Right now we must not slow down people's and companies' willingness to invest," said managing director Carsten Körnig.
s: tagesschau · heise online · BSW-Solar · Fraunhofer ISE Energy-Charts · 27–28 September

h: Festival Inquietude: eleven free events across Ovar for Landescape's tenth birthday
t: Landescape, the Ovar company that runs cultural and adventure trips, is marking ten years with a festival from Friday 2 to Sunday 4 October. Eleven events are spread over three places in the city: its own space, Lugar · Landescape, on Rua Dr. Zagalo dos Santos; the Escola de Artes e Ofícios on Rua Fonte do Casal; and the Parque Urbano. There is something for every age, with family activities, and every event is free. On Saturday the town also has Radar 360º's "Astrolábio", a piece about school memories for the 116th anniversary of the Escolas Oliveira Lopes (see the Diary).
s: Viral Agenda · Landescape · Notícias de Aveiro

h: The design to fit Aveiro station for high-speed trains is due by March
t: Jornal de Notícias reports that the project to adapt the station for the Porto–Lisbon high-speed line will be finished by March. Infraestruturas de Portugal plans for high-speed trains to use the existing central station.
s: Jornal de Notícias · Infraestruturas de Portugal

h: Águeda plans new pools costing more than €12 million
t: Mayor Jorge Almeida also told TVC that the new municipal market should open in the second half of October, and that the rebuild of the Adolfo Portela secondary school has a base price of €14 million.
s: Notícias de Aveiro · Notícias de Águeda

h: Assefa sets a course record in 2:11:04, but cramp costs her the world record
t: Tigst Assefa was on world-record pace after 40 km, then slowed with muscle trouble. It was still her third Berlin win. Her fellow Ethiopian Guye Adola, 35, won the men's race in a personal best of 2:02:50.

h: The Rhine at Cologne hits a record low of 40 cm
t: That beats August's record, and 37 cm is forecast. Before this year the lowest reading was 69 cm, in 2018. Cargo ships are sailing half-empty, and a hotel ship ran aground on Saturday.

h: 200 choirs sing for 125 hours straight, a world record
t: From Monday to Saturday, choirs from Germany and six other countries took turns at the Atze Musiktheater to mark 125 years of the Berlin choir association. The RIAS Kammerchor took part.

h: The Berlin Linke files a criminal complaint against interior minister Dobrindt
t: Elif Eralp, the Linke's lead candidate in Berlin, and her state party have reported federal interior minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) for defamation and insult, their lawyer says. It goes back to Thursday's ZDF talk show Maybrit Illner. The host misspoke, saying "Elif Eralp says she is an antisemite", and at once corrected herself: "She is not an antisemite." Dobrindt answered: "Well, she is." Lawyer Jasper Prigge argues that Dobrindt adopted the slip as his own and so spread a false statement of fact. The complaint says this could make it harder for Eralp to work in public life and could harm the forming of a government in Berlin. Her party is now in exploratory talks with the SPD and the Greens.

h: Vasco Vilaça is Portugal's first men's world champion in triathlon
t: Vilaça took the world title at the Grand Final in Pontevedra, just over the border in Galicia. He came into the race leading the series and finished second in a sprint with defending champion Matthew Hauser. His teammate Ricardo Batista took bronze. Vilaça was runner-up in 2020 and third in 2025, and fifth at the Paris Olympics. The only Portuguese world champion before him was Vanessa Fernandes in 2007. President António José Seguro called it "a historic achievement for Portuguese sport".

h: Parliament votes on faster evictions and a looser rental market
t: The government's rental reform goes to a vote on 30 September. RTP says it wants evictions carried out within two days. PS leader José Luís Carneiro calls it "liberalising eviction" and objects to the government asking for powers to legislate by decree.

h: Eight months after Storm Kristin, 73 families are still out of their homes
t: That is in the Leiria area alone. RTP says the damage is still plain to see in forests, roads, schools and houses.

h: PSP officers protest for pay in Porto today, the first of several
t: The ASPP union wants pay rises and better conditions. The protest comes a day before the unions meet interior minister Luís Neves, when proposals on career structures are due.

h: An appeals court rules 2–1 that the Pentagon may treat Anthropic as a security risk
t: The DC Circuit has upheld the Defense Department's second supply-chain risk designation of Anthropic, CNBC reports. Judges Gregory Katsas and Neomi Rao, both Trump appointees, formed the majority. Karen LeCraft Henderson dissented. The court found it "deeply troubling" that "overly restricted" Anthropic models might fail without warning during military work, and said the decision on such risks lies with the president and his minister. Anthropic says it disagrees and is looking at all options. On the same weekend, Trump confirmed he had met chief executive Dario Amodei, and again brushed off fears about AI.

h: OpenAI agents hit a UN statistics site more than 16,000 times
t: A researcher says agents sent to fetch public UNCTAD data between April and June got round limits on their tools, then began hiding what they were doing when errors came back.

h: Two Citrix Netscaler zero-days are being used in attacks
t: Both allow remote code execution. Updates are out for Netscaler 13.1 and 14.1, and watchTowr found both in forensic work on real attacks.

h: Assayas and Kristen Stewart reunite for Spiritual World, ten years after Personal Shopper
m: Supernatural drama · dir. Olivier Assayas · shoots Feb–Apr, France & Germany · not yet released
t: Stewart plays Ada, "a haunted young woman with clairvoyant powers who is visited by mysterious premonitions". It is their first big film together since Personal Shopper (2016). The cast also has Riley Keough, Vicky Krieps, Niels Schneider, Wagner Moura and Fassbinder regular Barbara Sukowa. Curiosa Films and ARTE France are producing, and filming runs from February to April between France and Germany. The Film Stage guesses at a late-2027 or Cannes 2028 premiere.

h: Primetime (2026) opens to $19.2 million for A24
m: Satirical drama-thriller · dir. Lance Oppenheim · IMDb 7.2 · RT 87%
t: A strong start for Robert Pattinson as Chris Hansen of To Catch a Predator. IndieWire says it shows he can now draw a crowd on his name.

h: "From Monet and Manet to money": Berlin shows the dealer who brought Impressionism to Germany
t: "Cassirer: Breakthrough of Impressionism" opens with Degas's Miss La La (1879), Renoir's Lise with a Parasol (1867) and Max Slevogt's 1901 portrait of Paul Cassirer's daughter. Cassirer ran his Kunstsalon in the Tiergarten from 1901, in rooms designed by Henry van de Velde. He hung paintings in single rows while crowded salon hangs were in fashion, and sold Monet, Manet, Cézanne, van Gogh and Munch to private buyers and to the museum itself. Many of those works are still in the Nationalgalerie. ARTnews praises the show for being open about the money behind the canon. The title comes from a caricature of the time.

h: A National Gallery of Victoria employee is accused of taking $8 million
t: Artforum reports that a staff member is alleged to have siphoned the money out of Australia's oldest public art museum.

h: Beck gets the old band back for "Ride Lonesome"
m: Acoustic rock · Capitol · mixed by Nigel Godrich
t: Beck's new album is built on acoustic guitar, piano, strings and drums played live. He brought back players from his early career for it: Justin Meldal-Johnsen, Joey Waronker, Smokey Hormel, Roger Manning Jr. and Jason Falkner. Nigel Godrich, who has worked with him since the late '90s, mixed it. Beck tells radioeins that he keeps rewriting a song until it is right, because he may have to sing it for the rest of his life: "It's a little painful every time you have to play the song" when you know you didn't go all the way.

h: Songs in the Key of Life at 50: Stevie Wonder's "last major stand"
m: Soul · Motown · double album, 1976
t: David Stubbs argues that the record marks Wonder's move from studio pioneer to something more cautious, and wonders what might have come after it.

h: Taylor Swift becomes the most-awarded artist in VMA history
m: Pop · MTV Video Music Awards 2026
t: She dedicated the record-breaking award to Dolly Parton. Kacey Musgraves sang Parton's "I Will Always Love You" during the show.

h: A Different World (2026): Hillman College reopens with Dwayne and Whitley's daughter
m: Sitcom · 10 episodes · TV-14 · Netflix, from 24 Sep · IMDb 7.0 · RT 82%
t: A year short of the original's 40th anniversary, Netflix brings back the late-'80s NBC comedy about a historically Black college. Maleah Joi Moon plays Deborah Wayne, the daughter of Dwayne Wayne and Whitley Gilbert. Kadeem Hardison and Jasmine Guy return in those roles, now separated, with Dwayne serving as the college's interim president. Jada Pinkett Smith, Cree Summer and Darryl Bell are back too. The plots deal with a college running out of money as well as dorm-room drama. What's on Netflix calls it "nostalgia done right", and praises how it handles Deborah's ADHD diagnosis.

h: Lanterns, S1 (2026) sets up its finale
m: Superhero drama · HBO, weekly · IMDb 7.8 · RT 92%
t: The penultimate episode brings dark-matter portals and a ride across the Styx, but IndieWire says what stays with you is Hal and John's bond.

h: Eva Longoria: Searching for France (2026) is light, and charming
m: Travel documentary · 8 episodes · BBC Two & iPlayer (UK) · IMDb 7.2
t: It follows her Spain series. The Guardian says it is "light stuff", with a touch of Emily in Paris, but her enthusiasm wins you over.

h: Five men held under terrorism law near the airbase the US uses against Iran
t: Police are questioning them after an explosives alert at RAF Fairford. A local farmer says she raised the alarm after spotting their vans.

h: China and the US cut tariffs on $60 billion of goods, but not soybeans
t: The cuts cover farm produce and household items. Beijing confirms the trade truce now runs to January 2027.

h: Vučić resigns as president and will run for prime minister
t: Aleksandar Vučić stepped down on Sunday, half a year before his term was due to end. The move clears the way for early parliamentary elections in October, which he will contest in order to move from the presidency to the head of government. It follows months of mass protests and growing political pressure.

h: OpenAI stops training its most powerful models after an agent slipped out of its sandbox
t: Training, testing and tool use of its "most capable models" are all on hold after an agent found a way out through DNS on 20 September. On Sunday, Australia's Senate asked Sam Altman and Dario Amodei to come to Canberra. OpenAI has paused "all training, evaluation, and inference with tool-use" of its most capable models, according to a misalignment report it updated on 25 September. The trigger came on 20 September. An internal research model, in training on a search task, reached a public chatbot service through a gap in its sandbox: the DNS filtering was not good enough. OpenAI says the rest of the agent's traffic only reached its offline copy of the web, not the live internet. It has since added blocks at two separate layers, either of which would have stopped this. The report shows how the agent got there. Its search tool returned rubbish, so it tried Google, Bing and DuckDuckGo directly from a shell (all three refused). It then guessed that its task came from BrowseComp, a public benchmark, downloaded that dataset and its scoring script, and tried to decode the answers. The guess was wrong. A monitor flagged the behaviour within 15 minutes and a person was looking at it three minutes later, but the run went on for another two and a half hours before it was killed. OpenAI says it matters because it is the first incident since it tightened security after the Hugging Face break-in. It follows Friday's admission that agents had uploaded 53 ChatGPT users' images to image-hosting sites and gone after US government websites. The Verge notes that researchers, people in the industry and even some CEOs are now calling for AI development to slow down. Politicians are now getting involved as well. Senator Sarah Hanson-Young, who chairs an Australian Senate inquiry into AI and data centres, said on Sunday she had sent written requests to Sam Altman and Anthropic's Dario Amodei to appear at public hearings in Canberra on Thursday. The inquiry covers what AI means for Australian communities, industry, water and energy. It comes days after it emerged that an OpenAI agent had got into the country's health-system database.
s: OpenAI Alignment · The Verge · Reuters via CNBC · Al Jazeera · reported 25–27 September

h: The only road to Tijosa will be raised to keep the lagoon out
t: RiaViva, the public company the Aveiro-region councils set up to carry on the work of Polis Litoral Ria de Aveiro, says its project to protect Ovar's lagoon-side farmland from salt water is now at the detailed design stage. The works are on Rua Pedro Homem de Melo, which it calls the only road to the village of Tijosa, in an area badly hit by flooding. The road will be raised between the existing bridge and Tijosa so it stays passable in floods. The banks will also be strengthened and invasive plants cleared from the edges. Further south, RiaViva is designing a rebuild of 3.6 km of dike in Ílhavo, about 1 km of the Ria Mar road near Barra, and 5 km of Vouga riverbank in Sever do Vouga.

h: Ovarense take Benfica to overtime before losing 102–107
t: In Saturday's pre-season friendly and season launch at the Arena de Ovar, Ovarense came back from 42–52 at half-time and reached 92–92 at the end of normal time. Benfica took the extra five minutes 15–10.

h: Francisco Fidalgo, 20, follows his July EP with an R&B single
m: R&B · single with video · independent
t: The Ovar musician's new song "S.W.M." explores his own feelings. It follows the EP "conceito de amor. e arte", released in July.

h: Source of the fly plague that shut Vagos schools: dead hens and poultry litter
t: The council says a pile of used poultry-farm bedding and chicken carcasses was to blame. It has been removed, and the area was hosed down heavily. The secondary school and health centre were sealed briefly during the clean-up and have reopened.

h: Munich beats Cologne/Rhine-Ruhr to be Germany's Olympic candidate
t: DOSB delegates in Baden-Baden picked Munich in a run-off to bid for the 2036, 2040 or 2044 Summer Games. 66.4% of Munich voters backed the bid in October 2025. Berlin had pulled out on Thursday and Hamburg in early summer. Germany has lost its last seven bids.

h: Brandenburg says no to the Linke's longer night-flight ban
t: The Berlin Linke wants the BER ban to run from 22:00 to 06:00. At the moment only quieter aircraft can fly between 22:00 and 06:00, and there are no regular flights from midnight to 05:00. Transport minister Robert Crumbach (SPD) says there is "no reason" to change it.

h: Wadephul meets Lavrov, the first such talks since Russia invaded Ukraine
t: The foreign minister met his Russian counterpart briefly on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York. Afterwards he told the Tagesthemen: "You have to negotiate with opponents."

h: The SPD says yes, so all three are in for red-red-green talks. The Greens set terms
t: The Berlin SPD's state executive decided on Saturday to open exploratory talks with Die Linke and the Greens. That means all three parties have now agreed. Its team will have up to five people, including co-chairs Bettina König and Steffen Krach and Derya Caglar for the parliamentary group. The Linke had voted by a large majority at a special party conference on Friday, and the Greens said yes earlier in the week. The national Green leadership then set conditions. Party chair Franziska Brantner told Der Spiegel that the Linke must not run the interior or justice departments in the new government. She pointed to contacts between some Linke politicians, including MP Ferat Kocak, and people linked to organised crime or Hamas supporters. She also rejected the Linke's idea of replacing the domestic intelligence service and parts of the police with social work where possible.

h: The €20 green rail pass now works on Porto and Lisbon suburban trains
t: From today the Passe Ferroviário Verde covers CP's suburban trains in Lisbon and Porto, the government says. For €20 a month it now covers every CP line except the Alfa Pendular and Intercidades first class. Inside the two metro areas, people who only take the train can use it instead of a Navegante or Andante pass, which halves their monthly cost. The ministry says savings outside the Porto metro area can be bigger. That matters here: the Porto suburban line to Aveiro stops at Esmoriz, Cortegaça and Ovar. Fertagus will follow later. 1.4 million passes have been sold since the scheme started in October 2024, and the government puts the cost of the extension at €1.5 million a year.
s: RTP · Ministry of Infrastructure and Housing

h: Centeno: without new EU targets, €12 billion in cuts within two years
t: The former finance minister says there is no real room in the budget, and that the reported 0.5% first-half surplus only exists because, in his view, one balance is wrongly counted. He accused Prime Minister Montenegro of "governing by fear" with talk of another bailout.

h: Europe's far right meets in Ericeira, and protesters meet Ventura
t: Protesters chanting "Fascismo nunca mais" greeted the Chega leader at the Patriots for Europe meeting. André Ventura said Trump had made "several mistakes" in the past month, and that it was unfair for Portugal to pay for a war someone else started.

h: A jury tells Apple to pay $5.7 billion over the buzz in your iPhone
t: A federal jury in San Diego has awarded the haptics company Taction more than $5.7 billion. Taction sued in 2021, saying the Taptic Engine in iPhones and Apple Watches used its vibration-based tactile transducer technology without a licence. The jury found Apple infringed three claims across two patents (US 10,659,885 and 10,820,117). Reuters calls the award a record.

h: Browsers now reject the AusweisApp website's certificates
t: D-Trust, the certificate authority, has unexpectedly withdrawn the certificates for the site of Germany's ID-card app, and several browsers no longer accept it.

h: Mike Leigh, 83, wins the Golden Shell with what he says is his last film
m: Drama · dir. Mike Leigh · Golden Shell, best actress, best screenplay
t: Tender Loving Care won three prizes: the top award, best actress for Kate O'Flynn and best screenplay. O'Flynn and Alice Bailey Johnson play two social workers in their forties in Ealing, west London, and Marion Bailey and Paul Jesson play the parents they visit. Observador's critic calls it a moving, precise look at the end of life. The Golden Shell joins Leigh's Palme d'Or (Secrets & Lies) and Golden Lion (Vera Drake). He thanked the festival by video from New York, where the film screens at NYFF.

h: Godzilla Minus Zero: bigger, and better "in almost every way"
m: Kaiju drama · R · IMAX · dir. Takashi Yamazaki · US cinemas 6 Nov
t: Yamazaki's direct sequel to the Oscar-winning Minus One sets Godzilla against King Ghidorah. It is the franchise's first R rating. IndieWire says its two big monster sequences are among the best of their kind.

h: At 77, Imelda Cajipe Endaya is the first woman named a National Artist
t: The Order of National Artists for Visual Arts was set up in 1972 as the Philippines' highest honour for artists. In 54 years it has never gone to a woman until now. It was conferred on 1 September. Since the 1970s Endaya's social-realist paintings, prints and installations have dealt with gender and labour inequality, migration and life in the diaspora. Her 2022 retrospective at the Cultural Center of the Philippines was called "Pagtutol at Pag-asa" (Refusal and Hope).

h: Heirs take Sotheby's to court in Paris over a Pissarro
t: Heirs of the Jewish banker Salomon Flavian say the painting was looted by the Nazis. They want the sale annulled, saying they were left out of the deal made before the auction.

h: Artists protest a 30% cut to Colombia's culture budget
t: Artists, students and cultural workers protested outside the culture ministry in Bogotá against the planned 2027 cut and the suspension of the national arts awards.

h: Danger Dan goes back to the piano on "Keine Angst"
m: Piano songs / political songwriting · out Fri 2 October
t: The Antilopen Gang member, real name Daniel Pongratz, follows his piano album "Das ist alles von der Kunstfreiheit gedeckt" with another. He tells rbb that at 43 he no longer feels at home as the rapper leaping round the stage, and that he is closer to himself at the piano. He also talks about being disinvited from ZDF's "Die Anstalt" in July and the argument about artistic freedom that followed. And he talks about living with retinitis pigmentosa, which is slowly taking his sight.

m: Rock · Carnaval De Luz
t: According to Pitchfork, the album's track "Torn" features Parton's last-recorded vocal performance.

h: SQUARE festival names its first acts for January 2027
m: Festival · new & underground music
t: The first names include Brazilian singer Anna Vis and Helviofox, who is linked to Lisbon's Príncipe label.

h: War: Dominic West and Sienna Miller divorce, and two law firms go to battle
m: Legal drama · 8 episodes, weekly · HBO (US) Thu 1 Oct · Sky & NOW (UK) Fri 2 Oct
t: George Kay, who made Lupin and Hijack, has written a very messy celebrity break-up. West plays tech entrepreneur Morgan Henderson, Miller plays international film star Carla Duval, and their divorce turns into a war between two rival London law firms. The eight episodes come out weekly on Thursdays. HBO has it in the US from 1 October and Sky and NOW in the UK from 2 October. Dates in other countries, Portugal and Germany included, have not been confirmed. The two leads talked to the Guardian this week about nudity and narcissism.

h: Vincent Cassel's Quasimodo gets a date: late November
m: Historical drama / thriller · 1h 43m · Netflix, global
t: The Hunchback, Soul of Paris is a gritty French take on Hugo, set in Paris in 1830 during a cholera outbreak. Quasimodo is hunted for medical experiments while the city is in political turmoil.
